JEFFERY M. WILKINS
Grand Master
October 10, 2021 - October 23, 2022

ii

Brother Jeffery Michael Wilkins was raised a Master Mason on August
27, 1992 in Lafayette Lodge No. 16 under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of
Kansas. He served as Master of that lodge in 1995 while stationed at Fort Riley
with the United States Army.
When Jeff was transferred to Panama, he affiliated with Gatun Lodge of
the District Grand Lodge of Panama under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge
of Massachusetts. Jeff served the District Grand Lodge as Grand Pursuivant in
1997 and Senior Grand Warden in 1998.
While in the Army, Jeff commanded the 911th Maintenance Company in
Panama and the Recruiting Company in Yakima, Washington. After 10 years of
service, he left the Army with the rank of Captain.
He then pursued a career in the semiconductor industry, applying his degree
in mechanical engineering from Rochester Institute of Technology. He spent
nineteen years working in the quality field from Quality Engineer to the Vice
President of Global Quality. In 2019, Jeff joined Collins Aerospace where he is
the site Quality Leader for the Propulsion Quality organization in Fairfield, CA.
After moving to the Bay Area, Jeff affiliated with Mosaic Lodge No. 218 in
Livermore. He served as Master in 2008. In 2015, Mosaic Lodge presented him
the Hiram Award. He is also a member of the Columbia Historic Lodge U.D. and
the Northern California Research Lodge, serving as Master in 2019. For the last
eleven years, Brother Wilkins has been active with the Grand Lodge of California.
He served as Junior Grand Deacon for Most Worshipful Larry L. Adamson in
2008-2009. He served three terms each as an Inspector and Assistant Grand
Lecturer. Jeff served on the Ritual Committee, the Lodge Support Committee,
and he was a facilitator for the leadership retreats. Jeff has also been a director
of the California Masonic Foundation, the Masonic Homes of California, and
the Nob Hill Masonic Center, serving as president of that board for five years.
He currently serves as a Trustee on the California Masonic Memorial Temple
and Acacia Creek Retirement Community.
Jeff is a 32° Scottish Rite Mason in the Valley of Oakland. He is a member
of the York Rite Bodies in Union City, Aahmes Shriners, Semper Fidelis Chapter
No. 135 Order of the Eastern Star, the National Sojourners, and Saint Francis
Conclave, Knights of the Red Cross of Constantine. For four years, Jeff served

5

ONE HUNDRED SEVENTY THIRD
ANNUAL COMMUNICATION

Friday Afternoon, October 21, 2022
The 173rd Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of California was called to order by Grand Master Jeffery
M. Wilkins on Friday, October 21, 2022.
Worshipful Brother Eugene L. Newman, Master of Mosaic Lodge No. 218
raised the Grand Lodge during the opening session using a gavel presented to
the Grand Master by his wife, Liz, and his children when he was installed as
Grand Master the previous year.
Reception of the Past Grand Masters
The Grand Master welcomed the brethren and directed the Grand Marshal to
present the Past Grand Masters of the Grand Lodge of California at the Altar.
The Grand Marshal then introduced each Past Grand Master, and the Grand
Master and Deputy Grand Master personally greeted each one. The Grand
Master asked the brethren to join him in saluting our Past Grand Masters by
the battery of three times three. The Past Grand Masters were then escorted
to seats reserved for them in the auditorium. The Grand Master then directed
the Grand Secretary to send to each absent Past Grand Master the usual letter
of greeting from the grand lodge.
Roll Call
The Grand Secretary was asked to call the roll of Grand Lodge Officers, Past
Grand Masters, and Past Grand Officers, and to ascertain if a constitutional
number were present to convene the Grand Lodge of California. The following
were present as indicated by their response to the calling of the roll:

Past Grand Officers

V\W\ Jack M. Rose  . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .  Past Grand Lecturer
The Grand Secretary announced that, according to the Credentials Report, there
were 957 Master Masons registered as of 12 p.m. Friday, with at least 20 percent
of the lodges chartered by this Grand Lodge represented, and that therefore a
quorum was present as required for the transaction of business.
The Grand Secretary reported that all lodges have paid their annual per
capita assessment to Grand Lodge.
Grand Lodge Opening
The Grand Master then opened Grand Lodge in ancient form. The Grand
Marshal and the Deacons retired to escort the flag of the United States of
America into the auditorium, which was followed by the Pledge of Allegiance.
Introductions
The following were asked to rise as groups for recognition:
Residents of the Masonic Homes and Acacia Creek, Diamond Jubilee Award
Recipients, Golden Veteran Award Recipients, Diamond Jubilee Recipients,
Hiram Award Recipients, Worshipful Masters, Lodge Secretaries and Officers,
Constitutional Board Members, Grand Lodge Committeemen, and District
Inspectors; each group was greeted with a round of applause.
The Grand Master also recognized Grand Lodge Officers visiting from
other jurisdictions.
Reception of Visiting Grand Masters
The Grand Master then directed the Grand Marshal to escort the visiting Grand
Masters from sister jurisdictions into the auditorium. The following were
received with Private Grand Honors and introduced:

The Grand Master welcomed the visiting Grand Masters to the Annual
Communication of the Grand Lodge of California, with the fraternal wish that
they would take back to their grand lodges a full measure of brotherly love
from California. The Grand Master directed the Grand Marshal to conduct
Most Worshipful Michael D. Johnson II, Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of
Kansas, Most Worshipful David San Juan, Grand Master of the Prince Hall Grand
Lodge of California and Most Worshipful Amir Ali Jandaghi, Grand Master of
the Grand Lodge of Iran in exile to seats in the East.
The Grand Master then directed the Grand Marshal to escort the representatives of grand masters from sister jurisdictions into the auditorium. The
following grand officers were introduced:

Grand Master’s Message
The Grand Master then relinquished his chair to the Deputy Grand Master for the
purpose of delivering the Grand Master’s Message (Appendix A). After his message, the Grand Master received a standing ovation and then resumed his station.
Grand Treasurer’s Report
The Grand Master called on the Grand Treasurer, Very Worshipful Charles P.
Cross, for his report (Appendix D).
Report of the Grand Secretary
The Grand Master called on the Grand Secretary, Very Worshipful Allan L.
Casalou, for his report (Appendix E).
Report of the Grand Lecturer
The Grand Master called on the Grand Lecturer, Very Worshipful Ricky L.
Lawler, for his report (Appendix F).
Legislation
The Grand Master called on the Chairman of the Jurisprudence Committee,
David M. Ferreria, for his report (Appendix K).
The Grand Master then called on the Chairman of the Finance Committee,
Levon H. Keshishian, for his report (Appendix K).
The Grand Master instructed the members of the established rules governing the proper protocol and manner of discussion on the various pieces of
legislation and proceeded with the legislation starting with Grand Master’s
Decision and Recommendation.

Saturday Morning, October 22, 2022
The Grand Lodge of California convened at 8:34 a.m. and, after prayer
by the Grand Chaplain, the Grand Master noted that Grand Lodge was raised
by Worshipful Brother Mark E. Pressey, Master of the Thirty Three Lodge No.
878 using a gavel presented to the Grand Master at the San Dimas Lodge No.
428 annual festive board.
Introduction of the District Inspectors

Video Presentation from the
California Masonic Memorial Temple Board of Trustees
The Grand Master directed attention to the video screen for the Report of the
California Masonic Memorial Temple Board of Trustees. The complete written
reports of both boards can be found in Appendix J of these Proceedings.
At 4:45 p.m., the Grand Master called Grand Lodge from labor to refreshment, to be called on again on Saturday at 8:30 a.m.

The Grand Master then directed the Grand Marshal to escort the District
Inspectors into the auditorium. The Grand Master thanked the Inspectors for
their continued service to the Fraternity and presented each of them with a

Memorial Service
The Grand Master called on the Very Reverend Steven H. DeMuth, Grand
Chaplain, to present a service of remembrance for our departed brethren. His
remarks were as follows:
My brothers, at this time we justly pause, remembering before God and
man, those worthy brothers who were called from their earthly toil during the
preceding year. I propose, through words and prayers, that we erect a fitting
tribute to our fellows who are now called from labor to their eternal rest.
Let us pray for them.
Into your hands, O merciful God, we commend your servants. Acknowledge,
we humbly beseech you, the sheep of your own fold, lambs of your own flock,
and receive them into the arms of your mercy, into the blessed rest of everlasting
peace, and into the glorious company of your beloved children in light. Amen.
Dear Friends: Let us pray for our brothers, that they may rest from their
labors, and enter into the light of God’s eternal sabbath rest.

12

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Receive, O Lord, your servants, for they return to you,
dust to dust, and ashes to ashes.
Into your hands we commend our brothers.
May they be welcomed into your dwelling place in Paradise.
Into your hands we commend our brothers.
May they gaze upon you, Lord, face to face, and taste the
blessedness of eternal rest. Into your hands we commend
our brothers.
May angels surround them, and patriarchs and matriarchs
welcome them in peace. Into your hands we commend our
brothers.
Almighty God, our Father in heaven, before whom live all who die in your
grace: Receive our brothers into the courts of your heavenly dwelling place. Let
their hearts and souls now ring out in joy to you, O Lord, the living God, and
the God of those who live. This we ask in your Holy Name. Amen.
In faith we entrust you to the earth from which you came. Our thoughts
and brotherly love accompany you and erect living monuments in our hearts:
Yet not to thine eternal resting-place
Shalt thou retire alone, nor couldst thou wish
Couch more magnificent. Thou shalt lie down
With patriarchs of the infant world—with kings,
The powerful of the earth—the wise, the good,
Fair forms, and hoary seers of ages past,
All in one mighty sepulchre. The hills
Rock-ribbed and ancient as the sun,—the vales
Stretching in pensive quietness between;
The venerable woods—rivers that move
In majesty, and the complaining brooks
That make the meadows green; and, poured round all,
Old Ocean’s gray and melancholy waste,—
Are but the solemn decorations all
Of the great tomb of man.
Let us also pray for all who mourn, that they may cast their care on God,
and know the consolation of his love.
Almighty God, look with pity upon the sorrows of your servants for whom
we pray. Remember them, Lord, in mercy; nourish them with patience; comfort
them with a sense of your goodness; lift up your countenance upon them; and
give them peace. Amen.

13

As our dear brothers have given us the gift of lives well lived, we now are
set to task, to hallow their example, and live the remainder of our days in the
pattern of God’s love for all mankind.
So live, that when thy summons comes to join
The innumerable caravan, which moves
To that mysterious realm, where each shall take
His chamber in the silent halls of death,
Thou go not, like the quarry-slave at night,
Scourged to his dungeon, but, sustained and soothed
By an unfaltering trust, approach thy grave,
Like one who wraps the drapery of his couch
About him, and lies down to pleasant dreams.

The Grand Master called on Most Worshipful Brother Melvyn B. Stein to
deliver the eulogy for Most Worshipful Brother Jack R. Levitt. His remarks
were as follows:

EULOGY
JACK R. LEVITT

Jack R. Levitt

Grand Master 1986-87
San Diego Lodge No. 35
October 2, 1995 - July 2, 2022

Most Worshipful Jack R. Levitt first saw this world on October 2, 1925
in Los Angeles, California. after high school he enlisted in the navy in 1944 and
served for two years on submarines. He then attended Pepperdine college,
worked as a movie projectionist, and received a college degree in 1949. Brother
Jack received his law degree from University of Southern California law school
in 1952, passed the bar exam in 1953; and in the same year became a master
mason in Silver Trowel Lodge No. 415 in Los Angeles. From 1954 to 1956 he was
a deputy district attorney in San Diego. It was during this period he married
his wife Kay. For 15 years from 1957 to 1972 he was in the private practice of
civil and criminal law.
In 1968 he became president of the San Diego county bar association
and thereafter, chairman of the state bar resolutions committee, president of
Defenders, Inc., and president of the San Diego Lawyer Referral Service.
At the age of 46, in 1972, he was appointed as a superior court judge by
then governor Ronald Regan. Most Worshipful Jack served on the national
panel of arbitrators for the American Arbitration Association, chaired the
California Judicial Council Advisory Committee, became vice president of the
San Diego County Law Library and Justice Foundation, presiding judge of the
San Diego Superior Court appellate Committee, chairman of the California
Judges Association Civil Law Procedures Committee (teaching many judges
advanced rules of evidence and procedure), and was a diplomate of the American
Board of Trial Advocates.
As a judge, he soon established a reputation of requiring attorneys appearing
in his courtroom to be timely, present and well prepared. For those who came
late, he rescheduled them to appear the next morning at 7:00 a.m.; and for
attorneys, that was just too darn early. Most counsel learned that Judge Levitt
would enter the courtroom exactly at the time set on calendar. There were few
who failed twice to be timely.
When an attorney presented a written brief on the law or facts and was
ready to make his oral argument, Judge Levitt would tell them that he had read
their briefs, and not to reintegrate what they had already submitted in writing.
This approach stopped many verbose lawyers who then became short on words.
In one case in which I was counsel, Judge Levitt asked the other attorney
to distinguish between two cases he had cited in his written brief. The attorney replied he could not do so as the document had been prepared by another
attorney. Judge Levitt had read the cases and wanted to know why the attorney
was referring to cases he had not read. Judge Levitt ordered the embarrassed

16

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

17

attorney to read the two cases and be prepared to present them in two hours
in court. No wonder, members of the San Diego Bar Association presented Jack
with a prickly cactus which Jack proudly displayed on his desk. He had become
known as “Cactus Jack.”
Masonically, Most Worshipful Jack affiliated with San Diego Lodge No. 35
in 1960 and became its master in 1979. He was also a charter member of Joseph
L. Shell Daylight Lodge No. 837.
In 1971 Brother Jack was coroneted a 33rd degree inspector general honorary
in the Scottish Rite, served as venerable master of the Lodge of Perfection, and
became, what we now refer to as the personal representative of the S.G.I.G. for
the Scottish Rite Valley of San Diego. he was also vice president of the California
Scottish Rite Foundation. He enjoyed being a Scottish Rite ritual cast member in
five different degrees, and on the Al Bahr Shrine ritual divan performing as potentate. He served for 18 years on the Grand Lodge Committee of Jurisprudence,
as sovereign of the Red Cross of Constantine, received the honorary DeMolay
Legion of Honor, and was a member of many masonic organizations.
Most Worshipful Levitt was installed as the grand master of masons in
California and Hawaii in October 1986.
The 1987 annual communication over which he presided involved many
controversial issues. There were 47 new resolutions, six carry-over matters, four
grand master’s recommendations, and four grand master’s decisions.
In June of his year as grand master he formed a committee of 15 members
to investigate the feasibility of the creating a grand lodge of Hawaii. During
the next annual communication in 1988, past grand master Levitt presented a
resolution to form such a grand lodge. The resolution was adopted.
One of the resolutions in 1987 sought to authorize the prohibited use of
a “cipher ritual” book. several committees recommended a “no” vote, but the
majority of the delegates voted in favor and the issue was carried over to the
next annual communication when the resolution passed.
The use of liquor in masonic buildings was presented in ten resolutions. Three were held over and seven were defeated. Grand master Levitt’s
Recommendation No. 4 was to allow meetings in buildings where liquor
was served. It was carried-over to 1988 when the delegates approved that
recommendation.
At the 1987 session of Grand Lodge, additional ideas were being discussed.
Among the resolutions not adopted were: to permit lodge business to be conducted in the first degree; accept advertising in masonic publications; and
to reduce the proficiency requirements in the three degrees to knowing and
understanding the obligations and modes of recognition.
Also during the 1987 year, many references were made to the United States
constitution, as it was the 200th anniversary of its signing. A masonic float in
the 1987 Pasadena Rose Parade celebrated that historic event.
Most Worshipful Levitt certainly had a challenging year as grand master, and
his theme for the year was to keep things moving and to “accentuate the positive.”

After moving to Montana in 1989 he affiliated with two lodges in Bozeman,
conducting degrees and acting as officers coach. he became chairman of the
Montana Grand Lodge Education and Research Committee and chairman of its
jurisprudence committee. He received the Montana meritorious service medal
and the distinguished service award.
Brother Levitt wrote: “my time on the bench taught me to be cautious in
making decisions and to be as accurate as possible when doing so. The fraternity
of freemasonry provided me with an outlet for learning, for expression, rich
friendships and a basis for inspiration. It provided me an anchor, in addition
to my religious upbringing, for my unfailing faith in god.”
Most Worshipful Levitt further wrote that his guidelines for life were:
“one’s word is his bond; to respect the person and property of others; to never
fail to keep a commitment...; to do what is right irrespective of any temptation; to place honor above riches; to perform any duty, no matter how small,
as well as possible; to be punctual; to not light my own candle by diminishing
another’s; to be clean in mind and body; and to forgo instant gratification for
lasting treasurers.”
Most Worshipful Jack R. Levitt laid down his working tools on July 2, 2022
at the age of 96 being survived by his two adult children, Steve, a master mason,
daughter Kristy and grandchildren.
He truly lived a masonic life; a man and brother of high moral and ethical standards, a man to be respected and admired; a man who adhered to the
dictates of our masonic charge — to be exemplary in the discharge of his civil
duties, paying due obedience to the law, practicing the virtues of temperance,
fortitude, prudence and justice.

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

The Grand Master thanked Most Worshipful Brother Stein and called on
Most Worshipful Brother Bruce R. Galloway to deliver the eulogy for Most
Worshipful Brother Howard D. Kirkpatrick. His remarks were as follows:

EULOGY
HOWARD DELANE KIRKPATRICK

Howard Delane Kirkpatrick
Grand Master 2003-2004
Reading-Trinity Lodge No. 27
July 14, 1935 - January 25, 2022

Most Worshipful Howard Delane Kirkpatrick was a longtime friend
and mentor, and I am truly honored to have been asked to deliver his eulogy. In
addition to being a friend to most who knew him, Most Worshipful Howard was
also a businessman, community leader, a masonic brother and grand master.
Most Worshipful Howard was born in Colorado in 1935 and grew up in
Oklahoma. He moved to Chico to attend California State University, Chico
after his discharge as an artillery sergeant in the US Army serving in Germany.
It was in what is now Chico-Leland Stanford Lodge No. 111 that he was raised
to Master Mason on November 21, 1967. On November 11, 1969 he affiliated with
Reading Lodge No. 254 in Redding. He lived in Redding with his wife, Jackie, and
their four daughters. Most Worshipful Howard owned an independent insurance
agency which still exists and is now owned and operated by two of his daughters.
Most Worshipful Howard had many admirable characteristics, but if I were
to pick one that truly highlighted his life, it would be his commitment to service: to his family, his community and to masonry. He served on far too many
boards and commissions to mention, however, I will say that he was elected to
the Redding City Council and served a term as Redding’s mayor. He was president and secretary of the Redding East Rotary Club. He was also a candidate
for congress. Somehow while doing all of this he found time to write a novel.
Most Worshipful Howard served as Master of Reading Lodge No. 254 in
1976. He liked to tell stories, and one that I heard most often was one he told
on himself. While serving as the master of the lodge, he received a call from
Grand Lodge. He was told that they had not received reports of the July and
August Stated Meetings. He informed them that Reading Lodge did not meet
in July and August. It was too hot. In fact they had never met in those months.
A very quick decision to rethink that policy was made.
Most Worshipful Howard served our fraternity in many capacities. He was
an Inspector for four years, a member of the Masonic Speakers Bureau and
active with the Leadership Retreats.
He was installed as grand master on October 15, 2003. He focused on strategic
planning and proposed the formation of the Grand Master’s Lodge. A supporter
of the youth orders, he and Jackie were particularly involved with Job’s Daughters.
After his term as grand master, Most Worshipful Howard returned to what
is now Reading-Trinity Lodge No. 27 as secretary for four years. It was my honor
to present the Golden Veterans Award to him.
Most Worshipful Howard was a big man, but he stood tall because of his
internal qualifications.
Soft and safe to thee, my brother, be thy resting place.

EULOGY
JOHN RICHARD HEISNER

John Richard Heisner
Grand Master 2018-2019
Amity Lodge No. 442
May 11, 1947–June 21, 2022

Most Worshipful John Richard Heisner entered into the Celestial Lodge
on June 21, 2022. A native Californian, he was born on May 11, 1947 in Dinuba
California.
After receiving his Bachelor’s degree from the University of Oregon in 1969,
John obtained his law degree from the University of San Diego School of Law
in 1972 and was admitted to the California Bar Association in 1973. He worked
as a Deputy District Attorney in San Diego for over 13 years before entering
private practice. Upon retirement he was president of his own firm.
John was raised a Master Mason in Eugene Lodge No. 11 under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Oregon on March 5, 1969. He affiliated with Amity
Lodge No. 442 in San Diego in 1985 and served as its master in 2004. In 2013
the lodge presented him with the Hiram Award.
He served masonry and our Grand Lodge for over 53 years. He was an
inspector, served on the Jurisprudence Committee, was a founding member
of the Public Schools Committee for San Diego. He served on all Grand Lodge
constitutional boards. He was appointed as Grand Orator in 2011 by Most
Worshipful Frank Loui.
Most Worshipful Heisner served as the 151st Grand Master of California
in 2016-2017. During his tenure, he led a contingent of over 170 brethren and
friends to Ireland, Scotland, and England to celebrate the 300th Anniversary
of the first Masonic Grand Lodge formed in London in 1717.
He was also a member of the San Diego York Rite Bodies, Al Bahr Shrine,
Southern California Past Masters Association, Red Cross of Constantine,
Rosicrucian College, a fellow of the Philalethes Society and a founding member
of Lux Lodge No. 846. In 2014 he was invested with the DeMolay Honorary
Legion of Honor.
Most Worshipful Heisner was also active in Scottish Rite. He served as
Venerable Master in the Valley of San Diego and was honored with the rank and
decoration of Honorary Inspector General of the 33º in 2011.
After his term as Grand Master, he served the California Scottish Rite
Foundation as Vice President and General Counsel. He was the Personal
Representative of the Sovereign Grand Inspector General for the Valley of
Palm Springs until his passing. He also continued to serve as Chairman for both
the California Masonic Foundation and Earl Warren Recognition Committee.
John married Margo Cook on April 17, 1982. They have four children and
nine grandchildren.
He was active in his community serving as trustee for the San Diego

22

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

Maritime Museum, San Diego Chapter of Saint Jude’s Hospital, and as an
Adjunct Professor at the University of San Diego School of Law. He was also an
author, publishing four books on the meaning of Masonic symbolism.
John will be remembered for his leadership, kindness, compassion, fairness
and humility. He was always willing to share his vast knowledge with others and
provided guidance when asked. His actions and thoughts were always for the
benefit of the Craft and masonry. He will be greatly missed by all who knew him.
Until we meet again – farewell, my brother.

GRAND MASTER’S BANQUET

Saturday Evening, October 22, 2022
The Grand Master’s Banquet was held in Grand Ballroom of the Fairmont
Hotel on Saturday evening, October 22, 2022 at 7:30 p.m.
Grand Master Wilkins welcomed everyone and congratulated the brethren
on another successful annual session. He then called on the Grand Chaplain
for the invocation.

their representatives, and their wives; the California Past Grand Masters and

Presentation of the Joe Jackson Award
This year, the Masonic Homes of California and our Grand Lodge were pleased
to present an award in memory of our late brother, Joe Jackson.
Joe Jackson, a Mason for 60 years and Hiram Award recipient, served Joseph
L. Shell Daylight Lodge No. 837 and Heartland Lodge No. 576 for 17 years as
secretary, assistant secretary, treasurer and chaplain.
Joe exemplified Masonic relief and brotherly love. He reached out to members and widows on a weekly basis; assisted with numerous applications to
MOS and the Masonic Homes; frequently called Masonic Assistance to check
the status of his member’s applications; and helped expedite the paperwork
process. He connected members and their families not only to Masonic services,
but also to community resources and programs for veterans. If Joe Jackson was
involved in providing relief, the outcome was guaranteed to be a positive one.
Through his tireless efforts and determination to improve and grow outreach, Joe was a catalyst for launching the successful Lodge Outreach Strategic
Initiative in Division IX. Joe passed away in 2012, leaving a legacy that set the
foundation for extending Masonic relief.

As we are all looking toward the future, I invite you to remember our
past. Job’s Daughters was founded in 1920 by Ethel T. Wead Mick during the
height of the women’s suffrage movement! This was also the time when the
19th amendment was ratified, asserting a woman’s right to vote. Mrs. Mick’s
vision of bringing together young women has developed into over 100 years of
empowering young ladies to realize their potential as leaders- much like in your
lodges, all over the world, where members are given a space to refine themselves
within a brotherhood of like-minded men. We, in our respective organizations,
share the same goals of building and crafting leaders by empowering individuals
to be their best selves and encourage confidence.
“Crafting Leadership” is such an important theme. It is so fitting that your
theme for this year and my theme “Bee the change you want to see in the world”
go hand in hand. As Job’s Daughters in California moves into its centennial

in speeches by masonic or eastern star members to the youth expressing that,
“The youth are the future. The future Masters in lodges, CEOs of businesses,

Miss Sydney Warney, Grand Worthy Advisor
International Order of Rainbow for Girls in California
Most Worshipful Grand Master Wilkins, officers and members of Grand Lodge,
distinguished and honored guests and friends of California Rainbow. Hello! I
am very honored to be here with you all today in beautiful San Francisco and
thank you for the opportunity to speak on behalf of California Rainbow. I would
like to introduce some of my fellow grand officers who are here with me today
and our state parents for Grand Assembly 2023.
Close your eyes and picture for a moment an early spring morning. As city
employees, government workers, and families dropping off their children begin
what they think is a normal day, then the ground begins to shake, buildings

36

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

37

begin to crumble, and windows across the city shatter. And then, all of a sudden,
silence. The day I just described was a reality for the people of Oklahoma City
on April 19, 1995. An act of hate, an explosion so loud it could be heard by people
nearly fifty miles away, took the lives of 168 people. That was the day the clock
stopped at 9:02 am.
This summer members of California Rainbow had the opportunity to visit
the memorial for the Oklahoma City bombing. The memorial stands as a place
of quiet reflection as it honors those who were killed, those who survived, and
those whose lives changed forever after the attack. While the memorial alone is
striking, one of the most impactful things to me was a large almost 100-year-old
American elm tree which stands in the Rescuers’ Orchard.
This tree, known as the Survivor Tree, bore witness to the violence that took
place that day and withstood the full force of the attack. The tree’s survival was
questioned by many, its trunk and branches were weakened by the explosion
and littered with debris and evidence. The tree easily could have fallen victim
to the attack, but despite everything it had faced, it survived. Its roots and its
one hundred years of history held it in place. Not only did the tree survive, it
grew and became a symbol of resilience and hope around the world because
like the people of Oklahoma City, with the support of both the local and global
community, it endured what most thought would break it.
Resilience is crucial in keeping organizations like ours standing for years to
come. Our roots, and the values and memories associated with them, have held
strong thus far because our members and the community that supports them
believe in the worth they hold. In order to keep our Masonic Family strong, we
need to go back to caring for our roots, and refocus on why we are here today.
What is it that makes you love your organization so deeply? What is it that
keeps you coming back year after year, event after event? For me, Rainbow has
always been my second family. A place where I am constantly surrounded by
people like me who have a passion for giving back and learning how to grow
as leaders together so we can make a difference in the world. We are bonded
in sisterhood and service, and it is this community and family that make us so
special. These are the unique qualities that will help us continue to stay resilient
through other trying events in our future. It is up to us to build the future we
want for our organizations.
The Survivor Tree never would have remained standing if it weren’t for the
people who believed in its value and the importance and history it held within
its branches. Like the tree, our organization isn’t able to thrive without adequate
support from people like you. If you believe in the importance and potential that
Rainbow has in developing the futures of young women please stand up. Now stay
standing if you have ever attended a Rainbow function. Continue to stay standing
if you have ever brought your daughter, granddaughter, niece, other female family
member or friend to a Rainbow event or if you have ever served on an advisory
board. Look at the people around you. This is the community that has truly helped
to keep us standing strong for the past 100 years. You can now all be seated.

In two short years, California will be celebrating the 100-year anniversary
of the first Rainbow assembly in our state, San Francisco #1, which opened in
1924. Much like the Survivor Tree, San Francisco Assembly is a representation
of California Rainbow’s history and strength as it has provided the roots and
inspiration for other assemblies to follow. It is a defining piece of California
Rainbow, and it is in danger. Currently, San Francisco Assembly has one active
member. If we don’t do something now, this assembly will fall. Its roots are in
danger and the impact of the potential loss of this assembly would be astronomical across all of California Rainbow. As we try to rebuild and retain our
membership, closing the first assembly would cause all others to lose hope. The
sisterhood our organization provides would be lost and there would be entire
communities of girls who would never get to experience the impact that being a
Rainbow Girl would have on their future lives. We need to work now to preserve
Rainbow not just for ourselves, but for the generations of young women that
will come after us. To those of you who stayed seated after the second question
I asked, those who have never attended a Rainbow function, now is your time to
stand with California Rainbow. There are over 330 Masonic lodges in California,
13 of those reside here in San Francisco. We are asking for your help. If each
Masonic lodge introduced just one new member to Rainbow, reached out to a
current member to encourage her to stay involved, or had one of your members
serve on an Advisory Board, the impact could be the difference in our survival.
If you stopped by our Rainbow booth during the past couple of days, did
you see the listing of all of the assemblies in California? I challenge you to reach
out and volunteer in some way so you can make an impact on the assemblies
in your area. Assemblies throughout the state are holding membership events,
fundraisers, and canned food drives. Make a pledge to support us and help us
grow, especially for those of you who live here in San Francisco.
San Francisco Assembly No.1 is our Survivor Tree, but it is only the beginning. With your help, its success can serve as an inspiration for growth and
rebirth for assemblies across California. Be the difference for California Rainbow.
Take a stand and you too will be a part of our history, our family, our survival.
Thank you again Most Worshipful Grand Master Wilkins for inviting me to
speak today. We hope to see as many of you as possible at our Broadway Bound:
A Glittering Marquee in 2023 Grand Assembly sessions which will be held in
Visalia, California from April 1st - 4th. Thank you.
Mr. Chris Arnold, Master Councilor

Grand Master’s Youth Support Award

Gary L. Ricafrente
Through good times and bad, Gary Ricafrente has been a champion for DeMolay
in his community. As a member of Gen. Douglas MacArthur No. 853 and Valley
No. 135, he has served in several lodge officers’ positions. But it’s his work with
the local DeMolay chapter that has been transformational.
Bro. Ricafrente was among the charter members of the chapter’s first
Advisory Council and served as its first Chapter Advisor. For that, he was
awarded the Zerubbabel Key by the organization. In 2015, he assumed the role
of Chairman of the Advisory Council, a position he continues to hold.
In 2020, the pandemic forced the chapter he helped found into an existential crisis. Through his unwavering leadership, Gary helped steady the chapter
and worked with new advisors to rebuild its membership. In 2022, the chapter
has grown significantly, adding 13 new members, with several more prospects
petitioning for membership. For that, DeMolay has recognized his devotion
to the youth order by investing him with the Cross of Honor for service as an
adult advisor.

They call Art Pasquinelli the “maker of Masons,” and for good reason. Since he
was first initiated into Freemasonry in 1968, he has been a trusted advisor and
mentor to generations of members. A past master of Golden Rule No. 479 in
1976, he has also served as officers’ coach since 2009, and was twice a Grand
Lodge inspector for his district.
In 1990, Worshipful Brother Pasquinelli was given the Hiram Award in
recognition of his lifelong work on behalf of his lodge. And in the 32 years since
then, he’s only continued to be of service.
Brother Pasquinelli’s importance to the lodge transcends titles or awards,
however. Instead, it’s embodied in his willingness to pitch in, no matter how
small or large the need. He often helps other lodges in his area as a coach or
in performing a degree, or even painting the walls. Just recently, he helped the
San Jose Masonic Center rewire its lights.
That spirit extends to his work on the Santa Clara Masonic Officers’
Association, which he has served through numerous committees, including
fundraising for several events. He often assists the district inspectors of the

is always available and ready to lend his hand—or his ear. He lends his counsel

than does Gerry Beller.
Brother Beller was initiated into Freemasonry in 1958 in Highland No. 748
and raised the following year. In 2004, he affiliated with Fox-Coates Daylight No.
842, which he served for many years as lodge chaplain. He is also a member of
the Al Malaikah Shrine and the Scottish Rite. Since 2021, he has been a licensed
Masonic funeral master, performing the sacred ritual with the required reverence
at more than 100 such events. In 2007, Brother Beller was recognized with the
Hiram Award; in 2009, he received his 50-year Anniversary Award. Now, at age
87, he has been in Freemasonry for more than 63 years.
However, it isn’t just his longevity that marks him as a leader among Masons.
Rather, it’s his ongoing efforts to provide and care for others that stands as a
testament to his belief in Masonic principles.
Brother Beller devotes much of his time to caring for elderly or distressed
members of the lodge and their widows. He drives them to doctors’ appointments. He takes them shopping. He brings them food. He maintains an extensive
list of lodge members and widows who he calls regularly—sometimes several
times a week—to check in on them. He keeps a stockpile of medical equipment,
including wheelchairs, canes, and walkers, that he lends out to anyone in need.
Brother Beller does this work without any thought of recognition or reward.
And yet his example speaks volumes and serves as an inspiration to all.
The Grand Master then gave his closing remarks and expressed his honor
and privilege at having been given the opportunity to serve the craft as Grand
Master.
The Grand Lodge Officers retired and prepared for the Installation of
incoming Grand Lodge Officers.

GRAND MASTER’S ANNUAL MESSAGE
Brethren of the Grand Lodge,
Our California Masonic Code, Section 404.130 (F) requires the Grand
Master to present at each Annual Communication a written message setting
forth all his official acts during the year, the general condition of Masonry within
this jurisdiction and his decisions and recommendations of legislation that
he deems necessary or appropriate for the welfare of the craft. The proceedings for this Annual Communication will contain the detailed reporting of my
stewardship of these responsibilities and powers with which you invested me.
Later today, I will separately present for your consideration the decisions and
recommendations which I have made or proposed. This afternoon, however, I
will report on the highlights from the detailed report, on the general condition
of our beloved craft.
A year ago, I started this Masonic year with the theme of crafting Leadership,
in ourselves, in our lodges, and in our communities. Our emblem–the beehive–made the theme come alive. The lesson of the Beehive from our ritual
reminded us of the core principle of showing up and working hard. The bees
are arranged in teams of 3, 5, and 7, and reminded us that leadership is found
throughout our craft and among our Entered Apprentices, Fellow Crafts, and
Master Masons. Throughout the year, we all met on the level. We showed up
in our lodges and in our communities and made a difference. We did this with
the help and support of our spouses and partners. As the bee and butterfly are
the pollinators in nature, we served as social pollinators this year. By showing
up and working hard, by being ourselves, and by living our values, we were
examples of leadership within our craft and in our communities.
By working full-time while serving as Grand Master, I hope I have been able
to model for our craft the important use of the twenty-four inch gauge, and
what it enables us to accomplish when supported by our Great Architect of the
Universe and a loving family. Leadership at every level within our fraternity is
accessible and possible with balance and a reliance on our higher power.
As I look back on the last year, I clearly see our growth as individual Masons,
as lodges, and as recognized and appreciated members of our communities.
I see this growth through the lens of our 2025 Plan. I’ll highlight our impact
through the plan pillars of True Friendship, Diversity and Harmony, and in
Positive Awareness.

48

True Friendship

Grand Lodge of Kansas, and the Grand Lodge of the Philippines. We also had
representatives visit the brethren of Alaska, Baja California, Hawaii, Washington,
Oregon, and Missouri. Attending the Grand Lodge of the Philippines was especially memorable for Liz and I, as we were able to take part in public ceremonies
to honor national heroes and to connect with the former California lodges that
initially formed the Grand Lodge of the Philippines.
Our relationships around the world are strong and we are especially united
in California and the western states and provinces.
Masonic lodges are places where diversity and harmony are meant to prevail.
Throughout history, Masonic lodges have been venues for people from different
parts of the globe and different religious, political, social and world views to
come together and work in harmony.
When diversity and harmony breaks down, a lodge begins to lose its Masonic
identity. It starts to look and act more like an ordinary social club powered by
cliques and personal ambitions. We must constantly strive to maintain harmony
in our lodges and maintain a diverse and compatible membership.
This year significant progress was made in restoring harmony to Van Nuys
Lodge No. 450. After four years of continuous suspension, I was pleased to
personally return the charter to the worshipful master. This was the result of
the hard work and dedication by the new lodge leadership, and of the support,
patience, and perseverance of their Inspector. For too long the lodge relied
on one brother to manage everything, which led to a lack of participation and
disharmony. The lodge reached a point where it did not have enough brothers
to open the lodge. Together with the inspector, the newly appointed lodge leadership dug deep into their roster and brought back experienced brothers and
they recruited brothers from other lodges to affiliate and fill key positions. As
a result, the lodge met every requirement to return the charter an operate as a
regular and well-governed lodge. If the lodge continues on this path, avoiding
any temptation to return to its former ways, it will have a bright future. This
serves as a reminder to all of us as Lodge brethren. It is we, the brethren, whose
suffrage puts individuals into positions of authority. Lack of governance and
oversight on our part can lead to disharmony and the type of problems that
result in the loss of a lodge charter. I want to congratulate the master, Wor.
Vahe Hamalian, and the officers and members of Van Nuys Lodge who stepped
up and provided important leadership. I also wish to thank the inspector, Wor.
Leland Celestre, for his good work.
As we close this year, there is only one suspended lodge. Fraternidad de las
Americas No. 867 in Union City has been unable to meet for more than a year.
The lodge could not assemble five members in good standing in order to meet to
surrender the charter. Tomorrow, we will consider the revocation of the charter.
Our diversity and harmony pillar also includes building stronger connections with Masonic organizations and youth orders. This year, I had the privilege
of attending several events with the York Rite, Scottish Rite, Shrine, Eastern
Star, Jobs Daughters, DeMolay, and the Rainbow Girls. I was especially proud

In visiting lodges throughout the state this year, I realized it was not the number
of lodge events that really mattered to me. What meant the most to me was
meeting my brothers on the level and establishing a connection – and a true
friendship. This year, I have been able to make new friends and to strengthen the
bonds of friendship with the ones that I’ve made before. Working in the Fairfield
area, it was a pleasure to visit lodges in the Sacramento area, the Central Valley,
Sonoma County, and throughout the Bay Area. These visits were for significant
events like 100th, 125th, or 150th lodge anniversary, installation of officers, and
the presentation of four Hiram Awards, four Golden Veteran Awards, and eight
Diamond Jubilee Awards. These visits also included degree conferrals and,
sometimes simply attending a stated meeting. With these visits, I was able to
create new friendships and connections with Temple Lodge No. 14 in Sonoma
and Santa Rosa Scottish Rite bodies. Here, we were crafting leadership within
ourselves. We are finding that our lodges are where our best friends are made
and where we can become our best selves.
Diversity and Harmony
One of our goals in the diversity and harmony pillar is to strengthen relationships with other grand lodges in California and across our border in Mexico.
This year, we developed and strengthened our relationships with our brothers
in the Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California. It was a pleasure to attend their Annual Communication and to enjoy times of fellowship
with their leadership over a meal. They have become a strong partner with our
Masons4Mitts teams throughout the state. We work together on the scholarship programs of the California Masonic Foundation. Together we celebrated
the 100th anniversary of the Stockton Masonic Center where our lodges from
both grand lodges meet and we had a wide variety of civic leaders participate
in that event.
For 43 years, we have joined with our brothers in Baja California and Baja
California Sur to celebrate our special relationship and learn from the similarities and differences of our grand lodges in an event called The Conference
of the Three Californias. This year, the Grand Lodge of California hosted the
conference in San Diego. The conference included the conferral of the First
Degree by Ignacio Zaragoza Lodge No. 3 and Cuauhtémoc Lodge No. 15, which
provided us insight into the ritual used in Mexican states and the opportunities
in could provide to us in California to experience it with them.
Additionally, we have made an extra effort over the last few years to establish
mutual recognition with all of the state grand lodges in Mexico, extending our
fraternal connections across the country. Later our grand secretary will report
on the considerable progress we have made with that goal.
In addition to the Prince Hall Grand Lodge, I was able to personally visit
the Grand Lodges of Iran in Exile, the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, the

the San Francisco Giants, the Los Angeles Angels, the Los Angeles Dodgers, and
the San Diego Padres puts us in the public eye as an organization doing great

Our support of public education this year included the celebration of the
Teachers of the Year in Sacramento and several public school events in Northern
and Southern California. I greatly appreciate all of the Public Education Advisory
Committees for their hard work in partnering with local schools to recognize
teachers and students as part of our September Public Schools Month. We are
proud to partner with national literacy leader Raising A Reader, which supports
our youngest elementary students by engaging families in shared reading routines at home. This year we are expanding to 84 new classrooms, bringing our
statewide total to 823 classrooms, well on our way to reaching our goal of 1,000
elementary classrooms in the state.
Lastly, our support of Masonic youth groups is a key element in creating
a positive awareness of Masonry within our communities. Our youth are the
leaders of the future for our craft and definitely are leaders today. I am proud
to have met and built relationships with these dynamic youth leaders. I can
learn as much about leadership from them as they can from me. I have found
that listening to their input and feedback is critical to providing the experience
that they desire and deserve. We are celebrating 100 years of Rainbow and have
just celebrated the same anniversary for both Job’s Daughters and DeMolay. I
am concerned that without changes, the next hundred years are in doubt for
these groups, and there is significant concern about even the next 10 years.
I would like to take the time to publicly thank all of those that made this
year possible. First is to my wife, Liz. Without her support over the past year,
I don’t see how I could have fulfilled my duties as grand master while working
full-time. Like all of the other spouses and partners, we are unable to be active
Masons without their support. I’d also like to thank Grand Marshal Chris
Trueblood and his partner, Brian, for their support throughout the year. To
the deputy grand master and grand wardens, this has been an amazing year
with excellent communication and coordination to ensure that there is solid
continuity in our leadership direction over the next several years. Our craft will
be well served by your leadership in the coming years. To the grand treasurer,
grand secretary, and the Grand Lodge staff, I am ever proud to have been able
to serve our beloved craft with you. Your professionalism is known throughout
the world and we are the benchmark for how a grand lodge should be operated.
You have been ever present with wise counsel and advice and I am extremely
grateful. To our grand lecturer, you have been able to ensure that we have come
back from the time of Covid shutdown with a spark for our ritual that will be
needed as we confer degrees upon so many men that have been waiting so
patiently to join our fraternity.
Lastly, to all the brethren of the Grand Lodge of California, thank you for
entrusting this important duty to me. I am eternally grateful for this time to
have been able to meet as many brothers as I have in so many different lodges.

Positive Awareness
Positive awareness is the third pillar of our plan. Through this pillar, we seek to
increase the number of Masons who share their membership with their families
and friends and increase awareness of our good work among the general public.
Like many of you, I took part in the “I’m a Mason” social media campaign
this summer, sharing with my friends the reasons I became a Mason. Because
of our combined work, tens of thousands of people read our stories.
We have also been active in our communities earning media attention. We
had media coverage of the Stockton 100th anniversary event with Prince Hall,
where the city historian, city council, mayor, assemblyman, and congressional
representative were present. At several other events, from Palm Springs to
Downey San Luis Obispo, Chico, and up to Redding and Eureka, we had civic
leaders present at our events and ceremonies. Our visit to the Philippines was
instrumental in raising positive awareness of Masonry in Manila, as our public
ceremonies were televised on local news.
Examples of our most public event, the laying of a ceremonial cornerstone,
were conducted in Eureka at the Veterans Memorial, in Chico at the Veterans’
Administration Clinic, in Redding at a Veterans’ Administration Clinic, at the
new Pavilion at our Masonic Homes in Union City, and at the Mayers Memorial
Hospital in Fall River Mills. We also dedicated the Sedam Terrace and broke
ground for the Veterans Memorial at the Masonic Homes in Union City.
Beyond our cornerstone ceremonies, we have had several opportunities
to raise the awareness of Masonry within our communities. In Susanville in
Lassen County, we rededicated the grave site of Brother Peter Lassen with
the local lodge, the Rotary, and Boy Scouts. We were also participants in the
Newhall Fourth of July parade and in the Nevada City Constitution Day Parade.
Our Masons Night at the Ballpark events provided significant exposure for our
craft, including on-field presentations, media interviews, and television and
radio coverage.
Getting outside of our lodges, our brethren actively supported their local
communities, like San Dimas No. 428, which raised tons of food and supplies
for the local food pantry in Twenty-Nine Palms. Elk Grove No. 173 contributed
thousands of pounds of beans and rice to the local community. Numerous
lodges sponsored Red Cross blood donation drives in their buildings at a time
of critical blood shortages. Old West No. 813 partnered with the Prince Hall
Dandridge Lodge No. 55 and the Red Cross on a blood drive. The Masons of
California came together in a time of need and contributed over $75,000 to the
International Red Cross in support of relief to the Ukrainian people. This year,
Masons4Mitts surpassed the $1 million mark in support for the San Francisco
Giants Community Foundation’s Junior Giants Program, as well as making
record-breaking contributions to our other MLB partners. This partnership with

Meeting you on the level as brothers has broadened my experience as a Mason
and made me so proud to be part of our gentle craft.
Masonry is a solitary journey that we take together. That journey requires
leaders to guide the way, provide vision, set goals, and make a difference. That
difference is found when we were “crafting leadership” within ourselves, our
lodges, and our communities. By building ourselves as living stones, we create
lodges that have the ability to be cornerstones of our communities.
Changing our communities for good through our works of service, building up our lodges, promoting positive experiences for our brethren, and living
our Masonic tenants daily clearly demonstrated that we were indeed “crafting
leadership.”
May the Great Architect of the Universe preserve and protect our lodges
and our ancient craft and keep you and your families in good health.
Fraternally submitted,

Jeffery M. Wilkins, Grand Master of Masons in California

REPORT OF THE
DEPUTY GRAND MASTER
2022-2023 GRAND LODGE BUDGET
Dear Brethren,
First, I want to thank the masters and wardens and other members
of the Grand Lodge for the support and confidence they have offered as I have
discharged the important duty of preparing the budget for the next fiscal year
of the Grand Lodge. At the last Annual Communication, the brethren approved
the per capita proposal, and this budget reflects our best effort to use that
per capita and other revenue sources to promote and advance our fraternity.
Therefore, I am pleased to submit this budget proposal for the period of
November 1, 2022, through October 31, 2023. This proposal will allow us to
continue our important programs and services and address our 2025 Fraternity
Plan priorities.
We now know to a fuller extent the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on
our fraternity. Some of the impacts were temporary, and we are all working
to overcome those. We lost just over 4,000 members due to our inability to
accept applications and confer degrees for 18 months. Our lodges are now
working to catch up and bring those who have waited into full membership
in the fraternity. We have also accomplished a good deal this year in creating
more positive awareness of our fraternity and connecting more interested
prospects to our lodges.
The loss of members presents a challenge on several fronts, including lodge
and Grand Lodge finances. Fortunately, the Grand Lodge has built reserves over
the past several years so that we can continue to provide programs and services
to members, lodges, and halls without an extraordinary burden on per capita.
This budget utilizes $398,134 of funds from the operating reserve. We estimate
lesser amounts will be needed in FY24 ($275,512) and FY25 ($195,146), with
remaining reserves to provide benefits for future years.
The important programs and services that will continue include:
• Professional public relations and communications efforts to create
positive awareness of Masonry; encourage Masons to discuss Masonry

• Financial services to lodges and halls including accounting, dues
collection, tax return services, and tax-exempt status restoration. The
cost of Intacct is included in the budget, so lodges will only pay an
additional amount for payroll services, if they use them.
• Real estate and insurance services and support for lodges and halls.
• Leadership training events including the Master and Wardens
Retreats, Secretary and Treasurer Retreats, Inspectors’ Retreats, the
Inspectors’ Leadership Retreat, Lodge Management Certification
Program, and the Speakers Series.
• Membership development efforts connecting thousands of prospects
to our lodges.
• New lodge development efforts, which so far have created 30 new
lodges in the state.
• Masonic education including support for programs like the
International Conference on Freemasonry, the annual Symposium,
and the Candidate Learning Center.
• Membership management through iMember, a GrandView product
now used by two-thirds of U.S. grand lodges.
• Ritual education and training including ritual conferences for inspectors, officers’ coaches, and lodge officers; and the annual ritual
competition.
• Communications to Masons, widows, and the public through lodge
website templates, the California Freemason magazine, the monthly
e-newsletter The Leader, all-member emails, social media, and new
video content, as well as the maintenance of over 125 lodge websites.
California Freemason magazine includes four quarterly issues and the
annual report.
These are all important programs and services that we will continue with
the adoption of this budget.
I appreciate the great work that has been done by our grand treasurer, grand
secretary, the finance staff, and our finance committee in assisting me in the
development of this budget. I also want to thank the masters and wardens and
other attendees at our spring leadership retreats, who provided good feedback
to me about this budget.
Brethren, I appreciate the support you gave in the adoption of the per capita
proposal last year. Our 2025 Fraternity Plan lays forth the prospect of a great

70

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

future for our fraternity. I ask you to join me now in adopting this budget as we
fulfill our obligations and enjoy the benefit of being Masons.

GRAND LODGE OF FREE AND ACCEPTED
MASONS OF CALIFORNIA

GRAND LODGE OF FREE AND ACCEPTED
MASONS OF CALIFORNIA

Fiscal Year 2022/2023
Randall L. Brill, Deputy Grand Master
Revenue Analysis

The Grand Lodge has several sources of income. Historically, the primary revenue sources have been Per
Capita and degree fees. The Grand Lodge Endowment Fund was created in 1992 and generates income
from the investment returns. To better manage the income from the Endowment, a 4.5% spending policy has been
instituted, calculated on a rolling five‐year market value average to protect the fund principle. The Grand Lodge has other
finance income, such as investment and interest income. The Grand Lodge receives dues from the Grand Master’s Lodge.
In 2004, the California Masonic Foundation included in its mission the funding of Masonic education and leadership
training programs and now provides a grant for such purposes. In 2005, the delegates of the 156th Annual
Communication adopted a $30 application fee to be paid to Grand Lodge by all applicants for the degrees of Masonry
and out‐of‐state affiliations. The Grand Lodge provides services throughout the state and receives reimbursement for
certain expenses incurred from the Masonic Services Bureaus funds. The Grand Lodge manages the investments of its
related entities and receives reimbursement equal to the cost of providing those services. The Grand Lodge is the sole
shareholder of the Nob Hill Masonic Center Inc. and receives dividends on the profits of this Corporation. The Grand
Lodge also receives support from reserves generated from prior fiscal years' surplus/operating reserves to balance its
budget.

The theme that appears on my logo is “Fulfilling Our Obligations.”
Those words seem simple enough but, in truth, for a Mason they are complex.
We Masons present this morning each knelt at an altar with our hands upon a
volume of the sacred law and, in the presence of our brethren and the Supreme
Being, committed ourselves to the high standards of brotherly love, relief, and
truth. Master Masons do that three times, which, in effect, creates a list of standards for which we each are held responsible. So it is impossible for my motto
to be taken literally. Instead, I am calling upon my brothers to focus on just
three commitments for the coming year. First is supporting our philanthropic
efforts, which is represented in my logo by the two dolphins forming a square.
I have a special place in my heart for those animals, which are great examples
of social beings that never hesitate to support each other and lend assistance
in times of need. Second is our commitment to supporting public education,
represented by the pencil and ruler, compass, and the volume of sacred law
doubling as a textbook—all representing the tools of nurturing a growing
intellect. California Masons have historically supported public education, and
that support is more critical today than ever. The final commitment, indicated
by the remaining symbolism in the logo, is support for the pillars of harmony
and diversity in our Grand Lodge’s long-range plan.
Philanthropy—the giving and sharing of our resources for the purpose of
helping others—is a part of every Mason’s DNA. To protect and provide charity
for our families, widows, orphans, and others in need or more broadly the family
of man, is a clarion call that none of us can ignore. At the local level, our brethren and their lodges have been creative and generous in establishing programs
through which they provide support—not only monetary but also through their
time and talent. Our lodges provide assistance in their communities and stand
ready to respond to unexpected needs, whether driven by social pressures or
natural disasters. I, my fellow officers, and the Grand Lodge staff know that
those efforts are ongoing and will continue well into the future.
But I am asking you, my brethren, and your lodges to do even more by
considering the wider community of those in need, and to support the efforts
of the California Masonic Foundation and our Masonic Homes. The latter is
a self-evident effort that directly benefits the members of our fraternity and

80

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

81

provides the best care possible for those who require assistance as they age.
The former, the California Masonic Foundation, is the umbrella under which
we support our local and statewide communities through charitable programs.
Throughout the coming year, you will hear me asking you to give what you can to
support the Homes and the Foundation. More and more frequently, our lodges
are making gifts in support of these programs, which is highly encouraging. But
I also want to encourage individual members to do what they can. Please keep
in mind that at the individual level, every penny counts. Whether you donate
$5, $50, or $500, every little bit helps. Between the Foundation and the Homes,
I hope that each one of us is fully aware of the positive impact that we have
on the lives of so many people through these efforts. Visit their websites and
learn about their impact.
Through the California Masonic Code, we are called upon to support public
education. Again, it is our obligation to answer that call. The quality of public
education in California has declined over the decades for several reasons, not
the least of which is frequent budget cuts and a sense of apathy among our older
citizens. In just about every community, the number of children that have lost
access to hands-on learning is growing. The pandemic has only exacerbated
those problems. Unless they’re assisted at an early age, these children will
struggle throughout their education. Our partnership with Raising A Reader has
made a significant impact on correcting that problem up and down our state.
At the other end of the age scale, our scholarship programs continue to help
students with limited resources achieve their dreams of a college education.
Most recently, we’ve added the Working Tools scholarship program, designed
to assist students who choose to follow a career in the trades. Given our country’s aging infrastructures and the declining number of skilled craftsmen, this
program will help fill the call for a much-needed resource. California Masons
are helping our children at both ends of the public education spectrum beat the
odds every day. All of this is in addition to the ongoing support that our lodges
provide local schools in their own communities. This continued support is vital.
The Grand Lodge of California has a successful history of creating and
executing long-range plans. With the valuable input of our brethren, we recently
created a vision that provides a path to our goal for the year 2050, “The World
in Harmony.” This year, I find myself at the helm in the middle of the current
five-year segment of that plan. During this current phase, we are supporting and promoting three pillars which were formulated with the input of our
California Masons. They are True Friendship, Diversity and Harmony, and Public
Awareness. While all three are worthy of your awareness, I have for the last
couple of years specifically championed the pillar of Diversity and Harmony. It
is my intention to continue to support those goals, though not at the expense
of the other two, because I have a true passion for it.
First, I will encourage and, as best I can, reinforce the traditions of our craft
because of the values they inculcate in our lives. I will not entertain efforts to
create shortcuts to membership and attaining our degrees or an easing of the

need to live up to our obligations. Let me point out that I see no current efforts
in that regard but be aware of where I stand.
Second, I will encourage quality and not quantity in our membership. We
went through a post-war era during which our lodges swelled in numbers but
eventually began to shrink in terms of actual participation. Hopefully we will
never take that path again. Ideally, lodge meetings and functions should attract
the participation of most of their members. Lodges are beginning to focus on
quality and not quantity in membership. A lodge of 50 or 60 active and engaged
members is much healthier than a lodge of a few hundred members, of which
only a small percentage are active. And a lodge that takes the time to engage
and get to know its applicants well before they are initiated creates a greater
level of participation among its members. Smaller lodges that are geographically
close to each other can create a network of support that are more effective than
what might be called a “mega-lodge.” You will be hearing more about efforts to
concentrate the impact of Masonry in our communities, partially through the
establishment of more, but smaller, lodges and through affinity lodges that will
cater to specific interests and activities among California Masons.
It was my father, Frederic A. Brill, whose example led me to knock on the
door of Freemasonry. The only surviving son of deaf parents, a WWII survivor
who literally served on the tip of the spear as the allies broke into Germany,
he experienced a plethora of life’s lessons which included an appreciation of
everyone he encountered, regardless of ethnicity or creed—not easy to maintain
given the social attitudes of his time. His example influenced both my brother
and I, and created in us a special kind of conscience. My father had close friends
who represented a diversity of cultures, and he cooperated with all of them on
several levels. Those lessons he taught through example have served me well.
I will be asking our lodges to look at their communities and ask one important question: Does the composition of your membership truly represent the
creeds and ethnicities found in your community? I understand that there are
areas that do not have a diverse population. But if your community reflects
diversity, does the membership of your lodge reflect it? If not, why not? Do
not misunderstand me. I will not be asking lodges to go out and recruit men
of different creeds or ethnicities or to achieve imposed quotas. However, I am
and will be asking that you work to make your lodge a beacon that shines for
all good men, regardless of their background. There are many good men out
there who hesitate to knock on our doors because of uncertainties about who
we are and how they might fit in. They need to know that you are there and are
sincerely willing to welcome them. Do not think in terms of casting a net to
pull them in—a situation which will inevitably end in sorting out the unwanted
portion of the haul. Rather, endeavor to make your lodge a lighthouse whose
beam attracts the curiosity of good men and makes them aware of who we are.
Don’t be a net; be a lighthouse.
Finally, I wish to point out something which you may not have considered
before. To all my brothers present, look around this auditorium and consider

82

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

how many of those present you have met before today. Is it none or just a few?
Neither. Each of us has met and knows all of the Masons in this room, as well as
others we may encounter anywhere in the world. How? Where? In a lodge room
kneeling at an altar like the one in front of us this morning. The altar may have
looked different and may have been located far away, but when we knelt there,
we were immediately connected with all our brethren around the globe. We all
committed to the same obligations which define our values and our attitude
toward each other, regardless of what race, creed, or social status we belong to.
Because of that, we know each other. We know that in times of need, we can
seek relief from a man we have never physically met before, because we know
he is a brother. I ask you this morning to never forget that we are a worldwide
network of brothers who share the same values and heed the same call.
With that in mind, you have my promise that my goal is to serve all of you
and enhance our mutual experience as Masons. I hope that I will earn your
support in accomplishing that.

REPORT OF THE
SENIOR GRAND WARDEN
2023–24 PER CAPITA PROPOSAL
G. Sean Metroka, Senior Grand Warden
As senior grand warden, it is my duty to present to you the per capita
proposal which will fund the Grand Lodge of California budget during the
fiscal year of November 1, 2023 through October 31, 2024. This per capita will
be collected next summer based on the number of Masons on the rolls of each
lodge on June 30, 2023.
As you know, the entire fraternity is recovering from the impacts of Covid19. The pandemic affected our lodges, halls, and the Grand Lodge in several
ways, including our finances. As the deputy grand master has explained in his
report, the Grand Lodge created reserves to help offset these losses without
an extraordinary impact on per capita. We will use these reserves over the next
few years to maintain programs and services that are important to our current
and future success.
I am optimistic that our membership will stabilize and even grow over
the next few years. This will help offset what could be the effects of continued
inflation facing all organizations. This proposal projects a slight increase in
membership in 2024. We have worked to keep expense increases to a minimum,
even during these times of continuing inflation. Total expenses are up only
1.34 percent from the FY23 budget. Increased revenue from new members and
the Nob Hill dividend will make up most of this increase. However, there is a
decrease in the operating reserve revenue by approximately $122,622, which
requires a $3.00 increase in per capita.
Therefore, the per capita I propose for the Fiscal Year 2024 is $60.50.
With your support of this proposal, we will continue our important programs and services, including leadership training and education, communications, technology, financial and administrative services, and the initiatives to
increase positive public awareness and membership growth.
The future of our fraternity is in your hands, brethren. Working together,
I am confident that we can create more positive awareness of our fraternity,

86

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

continue to improve the organization, and grow and prosper. I look forward to
being on this journey with you.
Thank you for your support.

remain effective and that our model for shared service costs is not only appropriate but consistent with best practices and within industry standards.

needs not only for our Grand Lodge entities but also for our Lodges and Hall
