REPORT OF THE
GRAND SECRETARY
Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of the Grand Lodge:
I am pleased to make this, my 15th report as your grand secretary. It has
been an exciting and productive year, as we began to rebuild and rebound from
the significant impacts of the pandemic.

Membership Information
Current Membership Statistics
As of June 30, 2022, we had 40,025 active Masons, including 2,663 Entered
Apprentices and 919 Fellow Crafts. Our Masonic family also includes 12,621
widows. Please refer to my written report for detailed membership activity,
by-law amendments, life memberships, and veterans’ awards.
We now have a clear idea of the membership impact of the COVID-19
pandemic. In fiscal year 2020, we were on track for our first year of growth in
more than six decades. Because we had to shut down lodge operations in March
of 2020, we were not able to process applications or confer degrees during the
months of March through June, which are usually the months with the most
degree activity. As a result, we had a small loss of 229 members, or 0.5 percent,
in Fiscal Year 2020. Because we could not act on applications during most of
Fiscal Year 2021 and because suspensions for non-payment of dues soared, we
lost just over 4,100 members that year, or 9.2 percent of our overall membership.
It was a rough year. However, we did come roaring back in 2022. Had we gotten
an earlier start, we might have achieved net growth, but many lodges struggled
to field degree teams early in the year. Nevertheless, we managed to record
more gains than in any year since 1995. With suspensions for non-payment of
dues still high, we recorded a small net loss of 457 members, or just about 1
percent overall. With what we now know, it’s accurate to say that we lost about
10 percent of our members due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
Moving forward, retaining existing members is vital to our growth potential. A current concern is the number of members who are suspended for

102

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

103

non-payment of dues. This year, just over 1,400 members were suspended,
which represents 3.5 percent of our membership. The average age of a suspended member was 53, and their average tenure was 32 years. Yes, on average
we suspended Masons who had been dues-paying members for 32 years. It’s
important to remember our duty, especially during challenging economic times
like the one we face now, to personally interview brothers who have not paid
their dues to determine the cause and to provide relief to those who need it.
A lodge may remit a brother’s dues, in full or in part, if he cannot afford them.
In surveying members who were suspended this year, we found that nearly 60
percent said they could not afford their dues. On top of that, 90 percent said
they were not aware they could ask for dues remission, and 77 percent said
they would have paid a portion of their dues and requested a partial remission
if they had known this option was available to them. Overall, 75 percent said
they would like to restore their membership.
Now more than ever, we must redouble our commitment to member retention. Let’s reach out personally to every member who has not paid his dues.
Let’s remind him of our ability to remit or partially remit his dues if he cannot
afford them. And let’s be sure he’s aware of the process for restoration if he is
suspended.
The restoration program we promoted over the summer produced good
results. In total, we restored 435 members. The coordinated dues-invoicing
program has also helped, allowing brothers to pay their dues quickly and conveniently. Statewide, 70 percent of our lodges have opted into the coordinated dues
invoicing program. These lodges collected dues from 12 percent more members
than did the lodges who did not participate in the program. If your lodge has
not yet opted into the dues-invoicing program, I recommend you consider it.
The cornerstone of our 2025 Fraternity Plan, and the focus of much of our
work this year, has been around increasing positive awareness of Freemasonry
in California. This work has been integral to our membership growth strategies.
We’ve learned from market research that most people seek information
about Freemasonry because someone they know is or was a Mason—mainly a
family member, friend, or mentor. Yet we also find that most Masons do not
talk about the fraternity to their family and friends. Many believe they are not
allowed to, while others are not yet comfortable talking about it. In order to
improve these outcomes, we executed three important initiatives this year.
First, we launched the #ImAMason campaign and asked our members to
change their Facebook profile picture to an “I’m A Mason” logo and post comments about their Masonic journey online. The campaign ran for just two weeks.
Hundreds of brothers participated. All together, we reached 2.8 million family
and friends with our stories. It’s amazing how a little effort goes a long way!
To help our members talk more confidently about Masonry, we designed and
published “A Simple Guide to Masonry,” providing every brother with information and answers to some of the most challenging topics in Masonry—namely
gender, religion, and secrecy. We’ve distributed thousands of printed copies of

the guide and a digital version is available online. The booklet is used as the
basis for our new training program on talking about Freemasonry, which we
rolled out at the Inspectors retreats this year and will continue in 2023 at the
various leadership retreats.
Talking about Masonry is fun and interesting, and data shows that it creates greater awareness and interest in our fraternity, which leads to our third
initiative, paid positive awareness campaign. For 10 weeks from July 15 to
September 30, we ran a paid social media ad campaign promoting Freemasonry
in California. The campaign served up nearly one million ads, drove 19,500
clicks to our website, and led to 3,775 requests for information about membership. These requests were processed through our all-new membership advising
process, which resulted in over 1,800 prospects being connected to our lodges.
A number of individuals were connected with other grand lodges as well. The
results exceeded our expectations. But there is important work that remains.
As lodge leaders, we must now follow up with these prospects. Officers of
the lodge have access to this information. Simply go to your dashboard on the
member center and you will see the list of prospects. Reach out to them right
away. Set up a time to talk to them and help them on their journey to learn more
about our fraternity. Let’s make this a high priority. Using a paid campaign to
generate prospects is ultimately only as effective as our follow-through. We plan
to run a similar campaign each year, so together, we’ll get better and better and
reach more and more people.
PROGRAMS AND SERVICES
Led by the 2025 Fraternity Plan, the focus of the Grand Lodge office is to provide quality services and programs, which reduce administrative burdens and
prioritize the member experience.
iMember 2.0
It has been two years since we partnered with GrandView Systems to roll out
iMember 2.0 and advance a national movement to provide a uniform system for
grand lodges and Masonic organizations throughout North America and around
the world. Today, more than two-thirds of the grand lodges in the United States
are using the system. The Grand Chapter of California, Order of the Eastern Star,
the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California, and Job’s Daughters in California
are also using GrandView. Grand Lodges in Africa and Australia, and Masonic
organizations like the Red Cross of Constantine also use GrandView. We are
now part of an international collaboration never known before in Freemasonry.
At a recent users’ conference, we saw a demonstration of a new tool called
Keystone, which will enable us to automate information requests between grand
lodges and Masonic bodies. For example, a grand lodge or grand chapter will be
able to use Keystone to quickly verify the membership of a California Mason

104

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

who seeks to affiliate with their lodge or chapter. This is just the beginning of
the benefits that come from working side-by-side with other grand lodges and
Masonic organizations.
It’s amazing how many of our members use the system. Today, nearly half
of California Masons are registered on iMember 2.0, gaining access to their
member record, virtual dues card, lodge rosters, Masonic education, and other
resources. The system will continue to evolve and improve. Training is an ongoing priority. In the next year, we will launch a new iMember training program
designed to get new users up to speed in a short time and allow members to
become superusers, mentors, and trainers themselves.

Communications

Member Services
Our Member Services team provides core support to lodges and members. Over
the past year, they processed more than 14,000 information and service requests,
a 20 percent increase from last year, completing more than 90 percent on the
first day with an average completion time of 150 minutes.
New Lodge Development
Our efforts in new lodge development continue to grow. Since the beginning
of this initiative, 32 new lodges have been instituted. Two were instituted this
year, making a total of six lodges under dispensation. I will give a full report
on charters tomorrow.
Financial Services
The Financial Services team provides accounting, budgeting, reporting, and audit
support for Grand Lodge and our related entities. Additionally, they provide a
variety of supportive programs and resources for lodges and halls.
Today, nearly 82 percent of lodges and 60 percent of halls are using Intacct
as their accounting solution and are receiving high quality service from the
Grand Lodge finance team. This year, Financial Services prepared and filed 580
tax returns for lodges, hall associations, and residents of the Masonic Homes.
Real Estate Services
Our real estate services team provided a full complement of property related
services to our lodges and halls and maintained the several Grand Lodge-owned
properties. The team finalized renovations at the Benicia Masonic Hall, the first
Masonic building in California; and completed refurbishment of the Quitman
Masonic Building in the Malakoff Diggins State Park.
The Grand Lodge maintains two cemeteries related to the Columbia
Masonic Hall in the Columbia State Park, the Columbia Masonic Cemetery,
and the Jamestown Masonic Cemetery. Plans are underway for the maintenance
and restoration of these historic cemeteries.

105

Our communications team executes a comprehensive strategy for our fraternity
through several websites, social media accounts, email campaigns, a monthly
leadership e-newsletter, and the California Freemason magazine, which once
again received national awards in the publishing industry. Our communications
team is also now producing very high-quality video content for use on social
media, websites, and in other communications channels. Of particular note are
videos produced this year on Napa Valley Lodge No. 93, Panamericana Lodge No.
513, and Kern River Valley Lodge No. 827, plus several other videos promoting
our programs and services. I’ll share a short clip of the Panamericana video to
give you a flavor of our new work.
Henry Wilson Coil Library and Museum
Interesting progress was made with the Henry Wilson Coil Library and Museum
this year. Please visit our newly designed website at www.masonicheritage.org,
where you can browse the library and artifact collection online. New this year
is our first digital exhibit, which you can view on the website. “From the Hands
of Brothers” is a collection of Masonic folk-art objects created by the hands of
self-taught artists who were inspired to share their skills and interest in Masonic
symbology with hand-made aprons, quilts, wood carvings, and mysterious boxes.
Our museum team also constructed a new live exhibit on display this weekend
on the mezzanine. Titled “Badges of Brotherhood,” this exhibit focuses on our
collection of Masonic jewels: officer jewels, Past Master jewels, Lewis jewels,
charity jewels, and others. A special feature is a collection of officer jewels from
our Gold Rush lodges.
RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
It is my responsibility to inform the Grand Master of matters pertaining to
foreign grand lodge recognition and to present to you, in the form of a motion,
the recognition of certain grand lodges that meet our criteria. The Grand Lodge
has received the following requests for recognition by foreign grand lodges:
Brazil. In Brazil, there is a national Grand Orient, a separate confederation of
27 state grand lodges, and a number of independent state grand orients, which
are separate and sovereign from the national grand orient. Our Grand Lodge
currently recognizes the Grand Orient of Brazil, all 27 state grand lodges, and
several of the independent state grand orients. We have received a request
for mutual recognition from the Independent Grand Orient of Pernambuco,
founded on December 2, 1926. This grand lodge is a member of the Interamerican
Masonic Confederation and enjoys mutual recognition with the two other grand
lodges in the same territory whom we recognize.
The Grand Lodge of California approved the petition and granted mutual
recognition with the Independent Grand Orient of Pernambuco.
The Confederation of Regular Grand Lodges of the United States of Mexico.

106

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

Freemasonry in Mexico is structured similarly to the United States in that there
is a grand lodge in each state. In Mexico, there are two additional national or
regional grand lodges. For years now, the Grand Lodge of California has sought
to strengthen our fraternal bonds with the Mexican state grand lodges. Today,
we enjoy mutual recognition with roughly half of them. Working closely with
the Confederation of State Grand Lodges to obtain requests and agreements,
I am pleased to be able to present to you today a motion to recognize all the
remaining state grand lodges in the confederation. Petitions for mutual recognition have been received from:

The Grand Lodge of California approved the petition and granted mutual
recognition with the grand lodges listed above.
One of the regional grand lodges in Mexico is the Grand Lodge of the Valley
of Mexico. We have enjoyed mutual recognition with this grand lodge for many
years. From time to time, the Grand Lodge of California has withdrawn recognition with the Grand Lodge of the Valley of Mexico due to invasion of territory.
Masonic recognition standards prohibit one grand lodge from forming lodges or
another grand lodge in the territory where a regular grand lodge currently exists,
except by treaty or other agreement between those grand lodges. Evidence has
been provided to our grand lodge that the Grand Lodge of the Valley of Mexico
has invaded the territory of the Grand Lodge of the State of Baja California, as
well as the territory of other state grand lodges. The Commission on Information
for Recognition under the Conference of Grand Masters of Masons in North
America reported in February 2022 that the Grand Lodge of the Valley of Mexico
does not meet the standards of recognition, and we find that the Valley of Mexico
no longer meets the standards of recognition by California.
The Grand Lodge of California withdrew mutual recognition with the Grand
Lodge of the Valley of Mexico.

REPORT OF THE
GRAND LECTURER
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Grand Lodge Officers, members of the
Grand Lodge, brethren all,
This is my fourth report to you, as your grand lecturer. My sincere thanks
and appreciation go out to all those brothers who continued to practice their
memory work during our Covid isolation period over the past two years. Because
of your efforts, our lodges were able to ramp up their degree performances to
accommodate all our candidates and brethren who had been patiently waiting to
receive their degrees. Thank you, brethren, for quickly and effectively bringing
our lodges back to life.
Many of our goals on the we had planned for our Ritual Committee were
holdovers from prior years. Now, in our first full year out from the pandemic, we
have been able to accomplish most of them. At our Ritual Committee meetings
in November and December, we outlined our tasks for the year. I received copies
of calendars from each of our district inspectors to ensure that lodge officers
were receiving the proper information for their planning efforts. We scheduled
our Master Mason seminars in Divisions II, IV, V, VI, and VIII. We restarted
our inspector conferences in the north and south. And we addressed the need
for further education for members who had been identified by their inspectors
and assistant grand lecturers as candidates to serve as officer’s coaches. Those
efforts also included members who had completed the Lodge Management
Certification Program to fulfill the requirement to qualify for their return to
lodge leadership stations. For the first time, we scheduled and completed the
first two Schools of Instruction devoted entirely to the promotion of music in
our lodges. And lastly, we celebrated the return of our 2022 Ritual Competition.

Master Mason Seminars
This year, we accomplished our goal of restarting the division Master Mason
seminars to ensure the consistency of ritual quality in our jurisdiction. My visitations this year included division Master Mason seminars at Oak Plains No.
789 in Sacramento on January 15 (Division IV), Bakersfield No. 224 (Division

126

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

V) on February 26, Arcadia No. 278 (Division VI) on April 16, and Redlands No.
300 on June 4 (Division VIII).

Inspectors’ Conferences

Calendars
Over the past year, I was able to observe several lodge events, including a first
degree at Mariposa No. 24 on January 22, visits to Gardena–Moneta No. 372
on March 4 and Redondo No. 328 on March 5, and a third degree conferral by
Valle De France No. 329 and Round Table No. 876 in Glendale on May 19 I also
attended an outdoor degree hosted by Live Oak No. 61 on the Sacramento River
and put on by the officers of the 222nd Masonic District, as well as third degree
conferrals at Aquila No. 865 in Roseville on June 21 and Sacramento No. 40 on
August 24. On October 15, I attended a special outdoor third degree put on by
our brothers celebrating the return to work at Paradise No. 124 following the
devastating Camp Fire.
With the information provided by our inspectors, several division and district School of Instruction visitations were part of my calendar this year as well.
Among those visits were to the divisional School of Instruction and ritual
competition for Division VIII at Temecula-Catalina No. 524 on July 16 and the
Division III multi-district School of Instruction events at San Leandro No. 113
on November 6 and the San Jose Masonic Center on January 29.
A big thank you goes out to the officers of the 935th Masonic District for
their fellowship and hospitality on the occasion of their School of Instruction
exemplification of the second section of the third degree at National City on
February 24; to Wor. Matt Enright and the officers of the 234th Masonic District
for their district school at Madison No. 23 in Grass Valley on May 10; and to
Wors. Joe Campbell, Jonathan Wong, Hercules Valdez, and the members of the
Santa Clara Valley Masonic Officers Association during their exemplification
of the second section of the third degree on August 18.
I also want to thank Wor. Rick Geyer and the officers and members of the
806th Masonic District for allowing me to give my presentation at their festive
board on September 3, and to the officers and members of Saddleback-Laguna
No. 672 and their master, Wor. Michael May, for allowing me to present at
their Masonic information night on September 22. Last but by no means least,
a special thank you goes out to Wors. Jeffrey Yates, Narbeh Bagdasarian, and
Jhairo Echevarria for arranging the beautiful, multilingual exemplification of
the second degree during the brotherhood degree at Burbank No. 406 on July 15.

127

In our first full year back, the Ritual Committee was able to conduct two
Inspectors’ Ritual Conferences. I’d like to thank the officers and brethren of
Hesperian No. 262 in Santa Maria for hosting our Southern California Inspectors
Ritual Conference on March 18 and the officers and members of Santa Cruz–
San Lorenzo No. 38 for hosting the Northern California Inspectors Ritual
Conference on March 25.
In addition to observing the inspectors exemplify their work at the ritual
conferences in March, the Ritual Committee met to record our thoughts for what
would become the agenda for new inspector training, based on the elements
found in our California Masonic Code section 405.030, “duties” of an inspector. The Ritual Committee gave input and time to facilitate the first inspectors
bootcamp for newly appointed district inspectors at the Inspectors’ Leadership
Conferences in San Ramon on August 19 and Irvine on September 23.
Several years ago, Very Wor. Jack Rose and the ritual committee received
survey information that showed a need and a desire to develop training for
our lodge officers’ coaches. That need was answered by the development of
the nine officers’ coach training modules, now available to the assistant grand
lecturers and district inspectors for their respective Schools of Instruction. At
our November and December Ritual Committee meetings, I requested that Wor.
Vic Ropac, assistant grand lecturer for Division VIII, oversee the development
of virtual modules to facilitate a need we identified for continuation training
of brothers who had gone through the leadership chairs of their lodge, and in
the process had completed the Lodge Management Certification Program.
One module has been completed so far, with the hope that two more will be
completed by the end of October, for use in qualifying brethren prior to installations this year.

Music
Covid has certainly gotten in the way of fulfilling our goals of bringing music
back into the performance of degrees over the past few years. Now, though,
in our first full year back, we have been able to plan and execute our very first
music School of Instruction event at Evergreen No. 259 in Riverside on July 23
and at Santa Cruz–San Lorenzo No. 38 in Santa Cruz on August 6. My sincere
thanks goes out to our grand organist, Wor. Stephen Miller, and to all those
brethren, families, and adult youth leaders who took the time to attend these
first schools to bring music back to all of our Masonic family. Both Wor. Steve
and I are looking forward to having more such events in the coming year.
My brethren, it is my duty to report to you and address the quality of the
ritual in our jurisdiction. For the most part, I am pleased with the attitude

128

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

and performances of the lodges I have attended, and with the performance of
those lodges I have received reports about. However the overall quality of the
ritual performed this year runs the full range from exemplary to very poor. It
is easy for me to describe events I observed that were the most notable, and
I will report on one such performance in a moment. But I have also observed
performances in which most or all of the brethren are not prepared, have chosen
not to rehearse before conducting the degree, or have brethren participating
that feel the need to demean our ritual in front of our candidates. I have fully
addressed each of these incidents of poor ritual with the relevant assistant grand
lecturers and inspectors. Regardless of your rank or title, I am asking each of you
taking part in the performance of our beautiful degrees to take responsibility
for your participation in the degree—in your preparation, in your delivery, and
in your respect for the candidate.
On the other hand, our Division VI assistant grand lecturer Wor. Alberto
Casanova and I had the privilege to witness something very special. A couple of
years ago, the officers and members of Round Table 876 made the decision to
perform the second section of the third degree in costumes, which they would
need to make. At that time, Wor. Al Moen and I ensured that their request was
made in accordance with established guidelines. Finally, in May 19 of this year,
Wor. Alberto and I were able to observe Round Table’s degree work with their
new costumes on the occasion of their assisting Valle de France No. 329 raise
a candidate to the third degree. After the performance, I spoke to them about
their meaningful and excellent work. They informed me that they wished to be
an example of ritual excellence in their area. I told them it was a bold move and
that every brother had to take on that responsibility for it to mean something.
That evening, every member participating in the degree agreed that they were
willing to take on that responsibility. My brothers, Wor. Alberto and I commend
each of you on accepting the extraordinary responsibility of ensuring our ritual
is being performed in a meaningful manner, and I wish you all the success in
your outstanding endeavor.

Ritual Competition
The 2022 Ritual Competition consisted of the master’s work at the altar, gavel
to gavel, in the third degree. There were 1,216 total word and floor-work points.
Would those of you who participated in this year’s competition please
rise. My brethren, thank you for taking the time to rehearse and participate,
and for sparking enthusiasm for our ritual. You are responsible for setting an
example for your brothers when you chose to participate at your district- and
division-level ritual competitions.
This year’s competitors came from all nine divisions, and 54 of our 108
Masonic districts. Here are the brothers who are our nine division ritual

GRAND CHAPLAIN’S MESSAGE
May the words of my mouth, and the meditation of our hearts, be acceptable
in thy sight, O Lord, our strength and our redeemer. Amen.
Before I begin any important endeavor, I pause and pray. Actually, Masons
are encouraged to do this right from the start. Before I write my Sunday sermons, I always pray, “Lord, give me a word for your people.” So when I began
thinking about what I wanted to say to you today, I asked God to give me a
good word to share.
Whether I feel immediately inspired or move forward by faith alone, I trust
God will be God and work with me and help me be a blessing. So imagine my
surprise when I uttered the words asking for a good word to share with you
and the next thing I saw was a billboard that read, “The quickest way to rise is
to lift up another.”
I don’t know why, but this quote stayed with me. As I sat ruminating, it
rang true. While searching for the attribution, I came across a portion of “The
Story of My Life and Work” by Booker T. Washington. “When I was a boy,” said
Washington, “I used to like to fight. I used to like to get a boy down in a ditch
and hold him there. But as I got older I saw that I could not hold him down
there without staying in the ditch myself. No nation can hold another down
without staying down itself.”
Washington went on to say, “I think I have learned that the best way to lift
one’s self up is to help someone else.”
This, for me, sums up everything I love about Freemasonry. Our craft is
open to men 18 and older who believe in a supreme being and are found to
be of good moral character. The purpose of Freemasonry is to make “better
men out of good men.” Within each of the degrees of Masonry, our moral and
ethical teachings are expressed and beautifully illustrated in words and deed.
Strangers become brothers and the bonds that form between them are lasting.
We are literally lifted up, raised up, and taught the importance of brotherly
love, relief and truth.
Central to our existence are ritual, acts of welcome, inclusion, and character-building. We vouch for one another, only partly based upon reputation, but
primarily based upon trust—even hope—that those who are drawn to become
better men will realize the value of symbolic Masonry, the value of offering a helping hand in the darkness, and an experienced guide along unfamiliar pathways.
I am enamored by the word “Resurrection,” in all its reverberations, with

134

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

synonyms such as awakening, renewal, restoration, revitalization. It is in resting
and rising, sleeping and waking, that we learn to believe and trust the Great
Architect of the Universe who has filled creation with images that point us
toward the mystery of life unending.
We experience a type of resurrection every morning, every springtime, and
every time someone gives us a helping hand. Yet I would like to suggest that the
secret of Masonry, the handmaid of religious life, is that “The quickest way to rise
is to lift up another.” This is similar to the axiom that it is better to give than to
receive, because in giving we always receive. We receive the blessing of participating in the divine plan of caring for our brother, and of following the Golden Rule.
Likewise, it is in lifting up one who is down—weighed down with any myriad
of weighty and wearying issues— a brother knows what to do. When I was raised,
I did not fully comprehend the mystery at first. It took time and experience and
learning to trust fraternal ties that convinced me of the value of what we do.
For example, a rabbi once said that “one who visits the sick takes away
one-sixtieth of his sickness.”
When we visit someone in need, we express sympathy and empathy. We let
them know that people actually care. Because a person’s physical state is often
related to their internal emotional or mental state, a visit can often improve a
person’s feelings in a way which literally makes them feel better, lifting their
spirit, lifting them up.
There is a song I’ve sung before that was made famous by Josh Groban,
“You Raise Me Up.” I’ve always assumed the lyrics were speaking about how God
comes to us in our need and lifts us up, setting us upon mountains, helping us
maneuver life’s stormy seas. But now, I believe that it also speaks of us, those
who have been raised up, who stand on the shoulders of those who have come
before and are raised up to more than they can be.
As I sing this song, I invite you to think about those who have raised you
up and helped form the person you are today. As you remember them with
gratitude, remember this: The quickest way to rise is to lift up another.
When I am down and, oh my soul, so weary
When troubles come and my heart burdened be
Then, I am still and wait here in the silence
Until You come and sit awhile with me.
You raise me up, so I can stand on mountains
You raise me up, to walk on stormy seas
I am strong, when I am on your shoulders
You raise me up to more than I can be.
Respectfully submitted,
Stephen H. DeMuth, Grand Chaplain

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

GRAND ORATION
Bee the Example—Build Leadership
Most worshipful grand master, brethren, and friends:
This weekend, we gather in the twilight glow of this Masonic year to indulge
ourselves in the enjoyable recollection of our recent accomplishments and in
fond tales of our departed brethren. Soon, we shall witness the dawn of the
next Masonic year, gleaming with the promise of better tomorrows. We express
gratitude because our blessings flow as fruit from the cornucopia. Within this
sacred space, peace and harmony prevail.
When we are done with our revelry and merrymaking, we will leave this
temple to mix again with the outside world. Out there, we have work to do.
Because out there, the world is not at peace and harmony does not prevail. We
see war overseas, political unrest at home, and a continuing degradation of
civil norms and discourse. Our neighbors may see all this and start to believe
that conflict is man’s nature. But we, as Free and Accepted Masons, know that
cooperation—not conflict—is man’s true nature. It is our better nature.
We know this because cooperation is a common thread connecting brotherly
love, relief, and truth. We know this because we have surveyed nature and have
learned great truths about cooperation within ourselves and in the divine plan.
We know this because of the lessons of the beehive.
The beehive is an emblem of industry and cooperation that reminds us
to be productive and to helpful to others in need. As bees are social creatures,
dependent on one another, working hard to fulfill their roles and obligations,
so too are people. We rely on each other to provide the love, protection, and
friendship that we all crave.
But the lessons of the beehive transcend our ritual. In one Greek tradition,
the creation of bees and honey are told as part of the wedding of Zeus and Hera.
It was a potluck affair with a prize for the best dish. The winner was Melissa, a
tiny bug with a body too big for her wings. Her small dish of pure honey won
her the right to ask Zeus for anything.
She explained how hard it was to gather enough pollen to make even the
smallest spoonful of honey and that she had no way to protect it. So she asked
for a weapon that killed with one strike, so that she might thwart would-be honey
thieves. Zeus scoffed at the idea of giving such a lowly creature the power of life

138

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

139

and death. But he nonetheless granted the request in his usual twisted fashion.
First, he made Melissa queen of her own hive, so that she may have thousands of helpers to make more honey. This ensured his own, ample supply of
honey. Second, he gave Melissa and her brood a lethal sting. But instead of
killing its target, it kills the user. A reminder that there is always a cost to pay
when resorting to violence, even if in self-defense.
Historically, it is believed that the origin of beekeeping occurred shortly
after, or concurrently with, the invention of agriculture in the fertile crescent of
the Middle East some 10,000 years ago. This is when prehistoric man became
small-scale farmers and learned to manipulate the lives of plants and animals
to make them more productive for human purposes. And even before that,
ancient man undoubtedly collected honey from wild hives.
In the Neues Museum in Berlin, there is a stone bas-relief carving depicting a beekeeper and several beehives. The carving dates to 2400 BCE and was
originally part of the pharaoh Nyuserre’s temple to the sun god Re at Abū Jirāb.
It shows that nearly 4,500 years ago, beekeepers in Egypt had learned to house
bees in artificial hives, use smoke to pacify them, and commercialize honey
production. The techniques shown on the carving are still used in some parts
of the Middle East.
Beekeeping was so important to the Romans that, in the first century,
Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella devoted book 9 of his 12-volume work on
agriculture to beekeeping. From it, we know the Romans made some modest
improvements on the Egyptian methods.
After the Roman period, beekeeping north of the Mediterranean developed
two diverging techniques. In heavily wooded areas like eastern Germany, Poland,
the Baltic region, and Russia, beekeepers kept their hives in trees. Often, natural
cavities in trees would be enlarged and trap doors added to allow for the harvesting of honey. In less wooded areas—like western Germany, the Netherlands,
Britain, Ireland, and France—beekeepers used an inverted basket for hives. This
basket is called a skep and is the distinctive beehive shape so common in popular
culture, which also lends its shape to Grand Master Wilkins’s pin.
The skep’s advantage over prior beehive designs is that it was easier to
move from field to field, which increased pollen collection, and thus, honey
production. But harvesting honey from a skep usually kills the bee colony.
The modern movable-comb beehive used today was pioneered in
Philadelphia by Lorenzo Lorraine Langstroth. His designs are portable like
skeps, but also allow beekeepers to inspect and harvest honeycombs without
killing the bees. As a result, production grew exponentially, and honey is now
commonly available.
And why do we care so much about bees and honey? Why devote so much
of this oration to myth and history? The beehive is a Masonic symbol, but it is
monitorial—left for later study.
Well, welcome to “later.”
It is unlikely that Masonry invented the beehive as a symbol. Rather, it is

more likely that we incorporated it from other, more ancient traditions. Thus,
mythical and historical origins of bees and honey help us understand why ancient
peoples valued them. This, in turn, may help us understand the Masonic beehive.
Likewise, we can look to our faiths for even more insight.
In the Old Testament, God describes the Promised Land as “a land flowing
with milk and honey.” The Quran says honey is the cure for each disease. In
Hinduism, honey is one of the five elixirs of life and several Hindu gods are
said to be honey-born. The Buddha consumed honey immediately before and
after his enlightenment. And honey was the prime ingredient in both ambrosia
and nectar, which were the food and drink that gave immortality to the Greek
gods. It is no wonder that man has always valued honey, and often associated
it with enlightenment, good health, and immortality.
But honey was not the only valuable commodity harvested from beehives.
For centuries, beeswax was also coveted for its use in candles, which allowed
for worship and reading at night; thereby providing two forms of illumination.
And yet, when we study the beehive, we see that bees make honey and
wax for themselves. They labor to ensure only their own survival—a seemingly
selfish approach. But by acting in their own best interests, they inadvertently
make the world a better place by pollinating the vegetation from which they
harvest pollen.
So, how do we translate the beehive’s lessons into our lives? How do we
earn our own sweet honey of enlightenment? By showing up, working hard,
and helping others.
Like the bee, we must focus first on ourselves. But unlike the bee, our
labors are not limited to sustenance. We must improve ourselves, which is a
much harder labor.
If we want others to practice brotherly love, relief, and truth, then we must
first practice them in our own lives. If we want peace and harmony to prevail
outside our lodges, we must first let them prevail in our own hearts. If we want
the rest of the world to denounce conflict and embrace cooperation as mankind’s
better nature, then we must first be the example and show the way, like a bee
showing others the way to flowered pastures.
When good men interact with society, they cannot help but spread goodness. Like a bee that goes from flower to flower, they go from person to person,
interaction to interaction. They share kind words. They show compassion. They
help people. And their goodness spreads. This is how Masons craft leadership.
This is how we pollinate the world with Masonic values. We improve ourselves
and then share our best selves with our communities.
But how can this possibly work? We are each just one person in a world of
eight billion! Are we really to change the world one person at a time?
Yes.
Bees pollinate the world one flower at a time, yet who can count the thousands or tens of thousands of flowers a single bee touches in its relatively short
life? So too shall we share our goodness, one interaction at a time. We may think

140

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

our progress slow, but Masonry is a progressive science. It works by small and
incremental improvement. We do not expect instant results when we work on
ourselves. Why would we expect anything different when working on society?
We improve our ashlars, but we never perfect them. We build pyramids, but
we never place capstones. We climb Jacob’s Ladder, but the top is always just
out of sight. We continue to hope that with time, patience, and perseverance,
our labors—our journeys—will eventually produce honey, for us and for others.
Even though we labor all our lives, we may still leave behind a world where
peace and harmony do not prevail. Because just as our individual work to
improve ourselves is slow and unending, so too is the work to bring peace and
harmony to all mankind.
We all serve at the will and pleasure of the Supreme Grand Master of the
Universe. We take instruction from His trestleboard. We cannot predict the
butterfly effect of any of our deeds. But we can have faith in His plan. For like
the ashlar, the pyramid, and the ladder, we must accept that we may not see the
work completed. And we may not even know the whole plan.
Yet, we shall not be discouraged. Our hard work yields progress. We see how
we make the world better—one person, one interaction—at a time. We see how
we help bring out the better nature in others. And our store of honey grows one
drop at a time. It may not sound like much, but a little honey goes a long way.
So, as the sun rises on a new Masonic year, let us imitate the honeybees
emerging from the hive in the early spring. Let us go forth into the world, mingle
with the stranger, act with charity, and leave things a little better than we found
them. And when we return home, let us return better men, looking forward to
the fruits of our labor, the spiritual honey of enlightenment, and the promise
of an everlasting morning in a pasture full of our favorite flowers.
Respectfully submitted,
Peter A. Ackeret, Grand Orator

GRAND MASTER WILKINS’S DECISIONS
AND RECOMMENDATIONS

Grand Master Wilkins’s Decision No. 1:
Clarifies The Provision Of The Title
Of Past Master
The California Masonic Code contains detailed provisions as to who may receive
the title of Past Master, including provisions for the resignation or death of
the Master. It does not, however, provide explicit instruction in the event
the Charter of a Master’s Lodge is suspended during his term as Master. This
Decision clarifies that, in this circumstance, the Master may not receive the title
of Past Master if he does not complete his term or serve until the installation
of his successor.
If you approve this decision, the following narrative will be added to the
appendix of the California Masonic Code in which the Grand Master’s interpretative decisions are recorded:
Interpretation of Section 805.020 of the California Masonic Code.
Title of Past Master
(2022 G.M. Decision No. 1)
If the Charter of a Lodge is suspended during a Master’s term of office, and
such Master is removed from office or does not serve until the installation of
his successor, then the title of Past Master shall not apply to him and he shall
not be entitled to membership in Grand Lodge, unless otherwise qualified.
Does not amend the Constitution, Ordinances or Ritual. Simple majority
affirmative vote required for adoption.

The Inspector or Grand Master may grant a dispensation to change the date
of a Stated Meeting, as provided Section 405.060 of this Code.

Grand Master Wilkins’s Recommendation No. 1:
Allows Lodges Meeting Less Frequently Than Monthly
to Conduct Certain Business in Alternate Months
At the October 2021 Annual Communication, the fraternity amended the
monthly Stated Meeting requirement allowing Lodges to choose the frequency
of Stated Meetings so long as they meet at least quarterly.
Reporting and other provisions in the California Masonic Code limit this
new flexibility by requiring Lodges to meet during specific months of the year.
Lodges that meet less than monthly must still hold Stated Meetings during the
months of February and August in order to receive annual and semi-annual
Lodge reports, and during the month of November to elect officers.
I recommend that these provisions of the Code be revised so that Lodges
can determine the meeting frequency that works best for it and still meet the
requirements of the Code by allowing a Lodge to conduct the required business at the Stated Meeting immediately following the deadline. For instance,
if a Lodge holds Stated Meetings in the months of March, June, September
and December, it shall elect officers in December instead of November. The
Treasurer and Secretary of such Lodge would make their annual and semi-annual
reports in March and September instead of February and August.
The recommended changes to the Code allow Lodges to decide what
months they meet. While they do not eliminate reporting or election requirements, they allow Lodges to meet deadlines without having to hold a Stated
Meeting in a specific month.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 807.000 of the Code will be
amended as marked:
§807.000. STATED MEETINGS.
A Lodge shall hold a Stated Meeting for the transaction of business at least
once quarterly, on the date (other than a Sunday) and at the time established in its Bylaws. The foregoing notwithstanding, Lodges whose Bylaws
provide for monthly meetings fixed by the phase of the moon shall hold a
Stated Meeting for the transaction of business once in each lunar month.
A Lodge may be opened for a Stated Meeting prior to the time fixed in its
Bylaws. However, no business shall be transacted prior to such time

In the event that the Master of a Lodge determines that inclement weather,
including but not limited to ice, snow, and flood conditions, or non-weather
related unsafe conditions, including but not limited to flood, fire, earthquake, civil disturbance and the like, existing on the day established in
the Bylaws of the Lodge for its Stated Meeting, makes it hazardous for
members of the Lodge to attend the meeting, he may, with the concurrence
and consent of the Inspector of the district to which the Lodge is assigned,
postpone the Stated Meeting to the same day of the week next following
the week scheduled for the Stated Meeting. The Master shall notify, to the
extent possible, all members of the Lodge residing within fifty miles of the
meeting place of the Lodge of the date of the postponed Stated Meeting.
Should a Stated Meeting be postponed, the business transacted at the postponed Stated Meeting shall be limited to the reading of the minutes of the
last Stated and subsequent Special Meetings, action thereon, payment of
the invoices of the Lodge, and such other business of an important nature
as determined by the Master to require immediate consideration. No other
new business shall be considered.
If this Code requires certain business to be conducted in a particular month,
and a Lodge that meets less frequently than monthly does not hold a Stated
Meeting in such particular month, then such Lodge shall conduct such
business at its Stated Meeting next succeeding such particular month.
Amendment to the Ordinances.
5/6 affirmative vote required for adoption.

Grand Master Weiss’s Recommendation No. 2:
Establishes The Lodge Executive Committee
as a Standing Committee
Our members tell us they are looking for more meaningful lodge experiences,
including more efficient and more engaging Stated Meetings. Many Lodges are
now using an executive committee to plan lodge meetings and ensure that the
Lodge is operating in an efficient and successful manner. The executive committee consists of the Master, Wardens, Treasurer and Secretary. Lodges with
executive committees have shown good progress in providing well planned
meetings and meaningful engagement for their members.
This recommendation provides a framework for all Lodges to benefit from
this best practice. This resolution does not, however, change the authority of
the Lodge to act and decide on matters before the Lodge as they do presently.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 806.000 of the Code will be
amended as marked:
§806.000. COMMITTEES.
A.

The Master and Wardens shall be a Charity Committee, and shall
have the power to draw upon the funds of the Lodge for any sum,
not exceeding $100 at any one time (or such greater amount as the
Lodge may from time to time provide by a standing resolution), for
the relief of a distressed worthy Mason and the wife, widow or orphan
of a Master Mason.

B.

The Master, Wardens, Treasurer and Secretary shall be an Executive
Committee, and shall meet at some time prior to each Stated Meeting,
at a time and place and in a manner designated by the Master who
shall chair the Committee. Its duties shall be to assist the Master
concerning the operation and affairs of the Lodge and to perform
such other duties as he may designate.

CB. The Master, at the Stated Meeting next succeeding his installation,

DC. The Master, at the Stated Meeting next succeeding his installation,
shall appoint a Member Retention Committee to personally, or otherwise, interview each delinquent Mason, ascertain the cause, and
work closely with the Master and officers in a continuing effort to
effect the retention of all worthy brothers unable to pay.
ED. The Lodge may have such other committees as the Master or the
Lodge may deem proper to appoint. All committees shall be appointed
by the Master, unless the Lodge provides otherwise.
FE. All reports of committees shall be in writing.
GF. Only members of the Lodge in good standing may serve on a Lodge’s
committees.

Grand Master Weiss’s Recommendation No. 3:
Permits Virtual Participation in Stated Meetings
At the 171st Annual Communications of the Grand Lodge, Sections
807.000 and 807.010 of the California Masonic Code were amended to allow
for entirely virtual Stated Meetings when assembling the required number of
persons for holding a Stated or Special Meeting is prohibited by government
authority. These amendments allowed our Lodges to continue to transact
important business during the COVID-19 Pandemic. With the withdrawal of
government prohibitions on private meeting and events, Lodges may now meet
in person. I hope we never again have cause to rely upon these amendments.
During the pandemic, however, we learned that virtual participation at
Stated Meetings provided opportunities for certain Masons to participate in
Lodge who in the past had been unable to do so or who could only do so infrequently or with difficulty.
This recommendation provides a path for Masons to continue to participate in their Lodge in-person Stated Meetings. This recommendation would
permit, but not require, Lodges to provide opportunities for their members,
Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts to attend virtually the business portion
of in-person Stated Meetings.
This recommendation does not permit Lodges to hold entirely virtual
Stated Meetings. A Lodge may do so only if the conditions and requirements
of Section 807.000 for an entirely virtual Stated Meeting are met.
In preparing this recommendation, I have considered a number of factors
from our brethren concerning modes of recognition and other ritualistic matters,
balloting, and the participation of officers and other Masons.
Regarding modes of recognition, which is to say the due guards and signs
a Mason displays when addressing the Master of the Lodge, a concern was that
someone other than the Mason may inadvertently view the modes of recognition
displayed during the business portion of a Stated Meeting. To address this, my
recommendation directs that the Lodge room camera be focused exclusively on
the Master, who does not return any modes of recognition when he is addressed.
As such, no inadvertent communication of the secrets of Masonry could be
revealed to a non-Mason in this manner. Other ritualistic participation, including
the conferral of degrees or examination of candidates, which include recitation
of oral sections of the ritual, as well as displays of the methods of recognition,
are not included as permitted activities for virtual participation. Within this
recommendation we have limited the participation to specific portions of the

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

151

Order of Business, which begins with the reading of the minutes, which occurs
after the ritual for opening the stated meeting, and ends with the completion of
miscellaneous and unfinished business, which immediately precedes conferral
of degrees and also the ritual for the closing of the Lodge. In the same vein of
thinking, no participation in virtual special meetings are included in the recommendation, as those meetings are intended for brief business subjects and
predominantly deal with the conferral of degrees and ceremonies.
Balloting is an important aspect of a lodge’s business, as well as the election
of an applicant to receive degrees or affiliate. As with previous virtual stated
meetings, this recommendation extends the ability for members to participate
in voice votes as a Lodge where the Master judges the outcome of the vote by
listening to the members vocalize their intent. In other ballots, such as balloting
upon applications using the ballot box, or other secret ballots, members participating virtually would be unable to participate in those votes. This is consistent
with the directions I provided with my directive on virtual stated meetings in
November of 2020. For these reasons, members participating virtually would
not be counted in the quorum of a lodge.
The Officers of the Lodge are essential to the business of the Lodge, and
therefore must be present when the Lodge is at labor. For that reason, all officers
of the lodge must be present. They may not participate in their officer position
remotely. That is to say, if the Mason who is the installed Senior Deacon of a
Lodge is unable to be present in person, the person who is occupying the chair
of the Senior Deacon in the Lodge room is the Senior Deacon of the Lodge at
that moment. This does not bar the Mason who is an installed officer from
participating in the stated meeting virtually.
I have left it to the discretion of the Lodge as how to best engage its Masons
virtually. The only requirement written into my recommendation is that the
Lodge room camera be placed on the Master, and not elsewhere in the Lodge.
This could be accomplished by a laptop on the Master’s podium or other means.
It would be permissible for the Lodge to display its remote Masons to those
in the Lodge room.
These are important matters to consider when continuing the virtual participation of Masons in our Stated Meetings.
If you adopt this recommendation, a new Section 807.005 would be added
to the Code to read as follows:
§807.005. LIMITED VIRTUAL STATED MEETING PARTICIPATION.
The Master of a Lodge may authorize the Lodge to allow its Masons to
participate in the business portion of a Stated Meeting virtually through
the use of conference telephone, electronic video communication or electronic transmission, provided that all of the following conditions are met:
A. Virtual attendance by a Mason of the Lodge at a Stated Meeting is
permitted only during the following portions of business as defined

152

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

153

in Section 807.030 of this Code:
1.

Reading of the minutes;

2.

Reports of investigating committees;

3.

Balloting;

4.

Reception of applications; and

5.

Miscellaneous and unfinished business.

B. During the portions of the Stated Meeting that a Mason of the Lodge
may attend virtually:
1.

Each Mason participating virtually in the meeting can communicate with all of the other Masons concurrently and is provided
the means of participating in the meeting, when recognized by
the Master.

2.

Each member participating virtually is permitted to vote on matters before the Lodge arising during the portion of the meeting
where virtual attendance is permitted, provided that the vote is
taken by voice vote, by hand or by rising vote. Members participating virtually shall not participate in any vote taken by ballot
and shall not be considered present for the purposes of any vote
by ballot.

3.

Video transmission, if any, to Masons participating virtually is
limited to video of the Master. Video transmission of Masons of
the Lodge participating virtually, if any, is at the discretion of the
Master.

C. No Mason participating virtually may fill an officer place or station.
D. A member participating virtually is not counted in attendance for
purposes of determining a quorum.
Amendment to the Ordinances.
2/3 affirmative vote required for adoption.

Grand Master Weiss’s Recommendation No. 4:
Negotiated Settlement at Mediation to Be Binding and Final
Mediation has become an effective tool for this Grand Lodge to settle
disputes among brothers and reduce the number of Masonic Trials for unmasonic conduct. This Grand Lodge formalized the process into the California
Masonic Code with its adoption of Grand Master Wright’s Recommendation
No. 4 at the 170th Annual Communication.
However, an accused brother may be reluctant to enter into a negotiated
settlement made during a mediation if he believes someone other than the
known accusers will bring charges on the same subject at a later date. It is in
this Grand Lodge’s interest that disputes among brothers be settled with finality.
A brother who has agreed to a mediated settlement should not be subject to
charges on the same subject matter at a later date. In my view, this result would
be unfair and a form of double jeopardy.
If you adopt this recommendation, the Code would be amended to permit
the negotiated settlement at the mediation of a charge of unmasonic conduct
to become the binding and final resolution of the matter. To protect against
potential abuse, the negotiated settlement would be a binding and final resolution of the matter only if after review it is so ordered by the Grand Master
with the concurrence of the Committee on Trial Review.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made to the
Code. Section 1404.570 of the Code which would be amended to read as marked:
§1404.570. DISMISSAL.
If in the Trial Master’s judgment all of the evidence introduced at trial,
taken together, would not warrant a guilty verdict on a charge of unmasonic
conduct, then he shall dismiss such charge. The trial record shall set forth
the dismissal and the Trial Master’s reasons for it. Subject to the provisions
of Section 1404.950 of the Code, sSuch a dismissal shall not prevent any
subsequent filing of the same or similar charge but with more evidence.
The Trial Master shall notify the Grand Secretary of such dismissal
and the reasons for it. The Grand Secretary shall then notify the Accuser
and the Accused of the action taken, as well as the Accused’s Lodge and
the Inspector assigned to such Lodge. If the Accused is a member of more
than one Lodge, the notification shall be given to every Lodge of which the

Grand Master Weiss’s Recommendation No. 5:
Transfer Of An Accused To The Grand Master’s Lodge
There have been many instances where disharmony within a lodge has
resulted from the actions of a single, disruptive member. This disharmony has
on occasion escalated such that the lodge’s charter has been suspended pending resolution of the matter. Rule 181 of the United Grand Lodge of England
permits its lodges by resolution to exclude any member for sufficient cause
with sufficient notice and a two-thirds vote. Sufficient cause can include an
allegation of disharmony or potential disharmony within the lodge. While I am
not prepared to recommend that California adopt a similar rule, I believe that
this remedy should be available in resolving charges of unmasonic conduct filed
against a disruptive brother. However, I also believe that the interests of our
lodges and of individual brothers in these circumstances should be balanced. If
the remedy at trial is exclusion instead of suspension or expulsion, the excluded
brother should not be in jeopardy of losing his standing as a Mason. To that
end, I believe that, when exclusion is found to be an appropriate resolution of
a charge of unmasonic conduct, the excluded brother should simultaneously be
transferred to the Grand Master’s Lodge so that he can maintain his standing
as a Mason with the right to petition another lodge for affiliation if he and such
other lodge so choose.
If you adopt this recommendation, the Code would be amended to allow
transfer of an accused to the Grand Master’s Lodge as a permitted resolution
of a charge of unmasonic conduct.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made to the
Code. Section 815.000 of the Code which would be amended to read as marked:
§815.000. GRAND MASTER’S LODGE.
The Grand Master’s Lodge is a special classification of Constituent Lodge
which shall be subject to all provisions of this Code applicable to Constituent
Lodges, except as follows:
A. There shall be only one Grand Master’s Lodge in this Jurisdiction, and
it shall be chartered with the name “Grand Master’s Lodge” without
a Lodge number;
B. The officers of the Grand Master’s Lodge shall be the Grand Master as

but also the per capita due Grand Lodge each year;

The Life Membership Fund of the dissolved Lodge shall be kept by Grand

Master’s Lodge shall cease for any reason, his life membership in the Grand
Master’s Lodge shall cease also.
The foregoing notwithstanding, if a life member of the Grand Master’s
Lodge is elected to membership in a Constituent Lodge which then offers
life memberships, his interest in Grand Master’s Lodge Life Membership
Fund shall be transferred to the Life Membership Fund of such Lodge. If
such member’s interest in the Grand Master’s Lodge’s Life Membership
Fund is less than the current cost of a life membership in the Lodge to
which he has applied, he must pay the difference within 60 days of the
notice of his election to membership. Upon his payment, he shall become
a life member of that Lodge. If he does not make such payment within 60
days of the notice of his election, he shall forfeit his interest in the Grand
Master’s Lodge’s Life Membership Fund to the Lodge to which he has been
elected. Should he later purchase a life membership in that or any other
Lodge, he shall receive no credit for these forfeited amounts.
The life member’s interest in the Grand Master’s Lodge Life Membership
Fund shall be equal to the lesser of the original sum of money paid to
purchase his life membership or his share of the fair market value of the
Grand Master’s Lodge’s Life Membership Fund at the time of his election to
membership in the Constituent Lodge which then offers life memberships,
as determined by the Grand Treasurer. In making this determination, the
Grand Treasurer shall compute the interest of each living life member in
the Grand Master’s Lodge’s Life Membership Fund and the interest of the
Grand Master’s Lodge in it, on a just and equitable basis.
The Life Membership Funds of every dissolved Lodge may be combined
into one common Grand Master’s Lodge Life Membership Fund at the
option of the Grand Treasurer or Grand Secretary; and
L. All other actions requiring the consent or vote of the Lodge shall be
effected by the Grand Master acting alone.

Section 1404.620 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§1404.620. PENALTIES.
The penalty upon a finding of guilt on one or more specifications shall be
fixed at one of issuance of a Demit from one or more Constituent Lodges,
reprimand in open Lodge, suspension for a definite period of no more than
one year, suspension for an indefinite period or expulsion, subject to review
by Grand Lodge as provided in Article 9 of this chapter. The penalty fixed
shall also be subject to the following requirements:
A. Absent mitigating circumstances, the penalty shall be set at expulsion
upon a finding of guilt on one or more specifications involving moral turpitude or the conviction of a crime involving a violation of the moral law;
B. Absent aggravating circumstances, the penalty shall not be set at expulsion unless there is a finding of guilt on one or more specifications
involving moral turpitude or another violation of the moral law or a
conviction under the criminal laws of the United States or of any other
governmental entity;
C. Absent aggravating or mitigating circumstances, the penalty shall be
set at suspension for a definite or an indefinite period upon a finding
of guilt on one or more specifications involving a knowing refusal to
obey the Grand Master’s authority properly exercised but which do
not involve moral turpitude nor another violation of the moral law;
D. Absent aggravating circumstances, the penalty shall be set at issuance
of a Demit from one or more Constituent Lodges or reprimand in open
Lodge upon a finding of guilt on specifications, all of which:
1.

Involve neither moral turpitude nor another violation of the moral
law nor a conviction under the criminal laws of the United States
or of any other governmental entity;

2.

Involve no breach of a fiduciary duty;

3.

Do not involve a knowing refusal to obey the Grand Master’s
authority properly exercised;

4.

Resulted in no material harm to Masonry or any individual; and

5.

Involved conduct not likely to be repeated; and

E. The penalty upon a finding of guilt on any other specification shall be
set as determined during the proceeding, subject to review by Grand
Lodge as provided in Article 9 of this chapter.

Gives the Grand Master the Right to Grant the Title

The proponents of this Resolution seek to give the Grand Master the right to
grant the title of Past Master upon a member that does not complete his term
as Master due to the suspension or revocation of his Lodge’s charter.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Lodge Charter Suspensions do happen from time to time; and,
WHEREAS, A Master of a Lodge may not be able to finish his elected term due
to a Charter Suspension; and,
WHEREAS, The Charter suspension circumstances may have nothing to do
with the Master; and,
WHEREAS, A Master has served and performed his duties to serve the Lodge
in spite of the Lodge’s Issues,

Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§404.120. POWERS OF THE GRAND MASTER.
The Grand Master may:
A. During the interval between Annual Communications of Grand Lodge,
exercise all executive powers of the Grand Lodge, except the power
to grant charters;

Resolution No. 22-04:
Modifies the Threshold Amount of a Contract
Requiring the Approval of the Grand Lodge Committee
on Masonic Properties
The proponents of this Resolution seek to increase the threshold amount of
a contract requiring the approval of the Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic
Properties from $25,000 to $50,000.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, California Masonic Code Section 406.060.D requires prior consent
of the Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic Properties if the expected cost of
any construction, alteration, improvement, replacement, repair, or maintenance
to a Masonic building is in excess of $25,000;
WHEREAS, this amount has not been increased since the year 2000;
WHEREAS, the California Construction Cost Index maintained by the California

164

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Department of General Services has increased by more than 127 percent over
the last 22 years;
WHEREAS, with the rise in construction costs, the present threshold of $25,000
is not appropriate for current conditions, being no longer adequate to cover
many of the routine projects that Masonic Hall Associations are required to
undertake;
WHEREAS, raising the threshold would reduce the burden of work unnecessarily incurred by Masonic Hall Associations, by the Grand Lodge Committee
on Masonic Properties and by the Grand Lodge Office staff, together with the
expenses associated therewith;
WHEREAS, removing barriers to the improvement, repair and maintenance of
Masonic properties would assist in improving positive awareness of the fraternity and further the aims of the 2025 Strategic Plan;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 406.060 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§406.060. MASONIC PROPERTIES.
The Committee on Masonic Properties shall consist of not less than five
nor more than twenty members. It shall examine and approve all details
regarding any contract involving a Lodge, Masonic Hall Association, committee, partnership or corporation or other entity representing itself to be
Masonic in character, or operating for the benefit of a Constituent Lodge
or Constituent Lodges for:
A. Any option or contract for the purchase of real property;
B. The encumbrance of real property;
C. The lease of real property, as lessor or lessee, for more than three years;
D. A contract for or commencement of the construction, alteration,
improvement, replacement, repair, or maintenance of real property if
the expected cost is in excess of $25,000 $50,000; and
E. Any option or contract regarding the sale or listing for sale of real
property.
The committee shall, subject to the approval of the Grand Master,
establish rules and regulations governing the processing of applications
for committee approval.
The committee shall review the reports of transactions of Masonic
Hall Associations submitted to the Grand Secretary as provided in Section
900.050 of this Code and may give counsel and advise concerning the
operation of those Masonic Hall Associations.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

taxes.

REPORT OF THE
BOARD OF TRUSTEES
MASONIC HOMES OF CALIFORNIA
The past year has largely seen a return to normalcy for the Masonic
Homes of California. For nearly two years, the organization has adapted to the
realities of life under the pandemic, from extended campus lockdowns to shifting to all-virtual service offerings through Masonic Outreach Services and the
Masonic Center for Youth and Families. Still, the success of the Masonic Homes
of California has been measured first and foremost by the health, well-being,
and safety of its residents and staff.
By that measure, the past year has been a success, despite continually
trying circumstances.
The challenges presented by the pandemic have continued to evolve and
affected each area of the organization differently. Despite that, the Masonic
Homes of California served more than 1,900 clients throughout California
this past year. That includes 292 seniors living on its residential campuses in
Union City and Covina; another 411 clients of the Masonic Outreach Services
dispersed throughout the state; and about 1,200 clients through the Masonic
Center for Youth and Families.
Transitioning out of the pandemic has come through fits and starts, as
it has been everywhere. Our residential campuses continue to operate under
local pandemic guidelines, but life has largely returned to normal. Many social
activities and communal dining have resumed, and the campuses have re-opened
visitation to the short-term rehabilitation facility.
That said, there have been several significant changes to the campuses—
perhaps none bigger than the opening in fall 2021 of the Pavilion at the Masonic
Homes. The Pavilion includes 28 apartments dedicated to those requiring
memory-care and assisted-living services, and is open to Masons and their
family members, as well as residents of Acacia Creek and, for the first time
ever, members of the public who do not belong to the fraternity. Through the
Pavilion, the Masonic Homes by bringing its high level of care to the wider
community. The new residence is filling quickly with current residents who
are now able to transition out of independent living, as well as clients coming
in from the surrounding area.

170

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

In addition to the Pavilion, the Union City campus also saw the reopening of
its newly renovated Adams Building, which has increased its capacity by nearly
25 percent to 48 apartments. Landscape upgrades and construction are ongoing
on the Wollenberg Building, which when complete will increase occupancy by
15 residents to 39. In Covina, construction continues on the new skilled nursing
building that will include 32 new apartments, divided evenly between memory
care and long- and short-term skilled nursing. Once complete, overall capacity
at the two campuses will have nearly doubled to 202 residents. The overall
increase in capacity is particularly important for the Masonic Homes, as the
waitlists for service at both campuses remain impacted. As of August 2022, 38
people were on the waitlist for services in Union City, including non-Masonic
clients at the Pavilion; another 26 were on the waitlist in Covina.
Elsewhere in the organization, the Masonic Homes has adapted to a primarily virtual paradigm effectively. Thousands of people were served over the
past year through the Masonic Assistance Line, which connects members with
counselors and staff who can help them identify and access resources and
emergency funds. Masonic Senior Outreach Services served more than 340
clients over the past year, helping elderly members access financial assistance
as well as help navigating outside services such as Veterans’ Affairs, AARP, or
Medicare benefits. The Masonic Outreach Services staff also made more than
800 calls to members in response to fire relief. Our lodges were supported
through Lodge Outreach meetings and skills-building workshops which trained
317 Masons throughout the year. The Masonic Value Network has also grown in
both scope and popularity. This program helps members research and access
healthcare options in their own communities and offers discounts by leveraging the Masonic Homes’ relationships with vetted home healthcare providers,
senior communities, placement services, and pharmacies. The prescription
drug discount service has been especially popular.
The Masonic Center for Youth and Families has expanded to provide
invaluable services as need exploded during the pandemic. Rapid expansion
of telehealth services has enabled MCYAF to provide therapy and counseling
programs to more than 1,200 adults, families, and young people throughout the
state in the past year. MCYAF has increased its support to Masons across the
lifespan, developing partnerships with the Masonic youth orders, presenting to
spouses and partners, and providing direct services to residents of the Masonic
Homes. In addition, the program—which once again received the prestigious
Praesidium child safety certification in 2022—has seen a radical increase in
interest in partnerships from outside community and Masonic organizations.
One particularly encouraging such partnership began this year with the Pomona
Unified School District, which contracted with MCYAF in a three-year, $250,000
agreement to provide services to students in their schools.
Partnerships like these represent an important way for the Masonic Homes
of California to bring its world-class services to even more people in need. As
such, the Masonic Homes continues to be an industry leader as a member of the

Thrive Alliance, an influential, national group on the forefront of the promotion
and research of innovative technologies for healthy aging. The Masonic Homes
also continues to support and collaborate with the Alzheimer’s Association,
the Child Advocacy Center, and other local civic and healthcare organizations.
Within the larger Masonic fraternity, the organization is committed to working closely with the Masonic Communities and Services Association and the
RiteCare Language Centers of the Scottish Rite. These kinds of partnerships
strengthen the reputation of Masons and the Masonic Homes in our communities and add to the awareness of the fraternity both close to home and on a
national stage.
As the Masonic Homes approaches the 125th anniversary of its founding,
it’s with that kind of an eye on bringing the highest possible level of care to its
community that the organization is plotting its future. Thanks to its foresight
and advance planning—and the adaptiveness displayed over the past two years—
the Masonic Homes of California is well-positioned to deliver on that promise.
The Board wishes to thank Grand Master Jeff Wilkins for his support; the
board of trustees for their vision and guidance, and Board Chairman Larry
Adamson for his leadership. As it has since 1898, the crown jewel of our fraternity continues to evolve and meet the needs of its community—as it will for
the next 125 years.
Respectfully submitted,
