REPORT OF THE
BOARD OF TRUSTEES
Acacia Creek Retirement Community
As the Acacia Creek Retirement Community enters its 12th year of
operation, its mission remains the same. To provide residents with an active
and meaningful life. And despite the challenges posed by the pandemic, Acacia
Creek is continuing to make good on that promise.
In 2022, the board of directors adopted a new strategic plan aimed at building on that foundation and propelling the organization into its next decade.
The plan is supported by four pillars: quality of life, operational integrity, board
engagement, and Masonic connections.
The ﬁrst pillar, quality of life, represents the well-being, safety, and happiness of residents. This has always been, and will always be, Acacia Creek’s
guiding star, around which all decision-making and programming is focused.
The second pillar is operational integrity, or the management of ﬁscal responsibilities. It ensures that the organization sets the right parameters in order
to meets its ﬁnancial goals. The third pillar is board engagement, aimed at
developing a culture in which the board is participating actively in the Acacia
Creek community. The ﬁnal pillar, Masonic connections, aligns Acacia Creek’s
mission and strategic plan with those of the larger fraternity. With these pillars
supporting its vision, Acacia Creek is primed to enter a new and successful
phase of its growth.
Over the past two years, the COVID-19 pandemic has played a dramatic role
in Acacia Creek’s operations, severely limiting the ability to tour and ﬁll vacant
apartments. Nationally, occupancy rates across all senior housing models stood
at just 81 percent as of the fourth quarter of 2021. Acacia Creek was not immune
to this trend during the pandemic, and its overall occupancy rate has dropped
from 96 percent capacity pre-pandemic to 77 percent as of August 15, 2022.
Increasing occupancy at Acacia Creek is the top priority moving forward.
While in-person tours were restricted during the pandemic, they resumed in
March 2022. Since then, tour activity has increased month over month. Bolstered
by a fresh look on our sales materials and website, the sales and marketing programs have focused on stimulating interest through phone calls with contacts
acquired through Acacia Creek’s direct-mail program and website referrals.
Retirement counselors are also updating members on the waitlist via phone,

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

193

virtual tours, and over Acacia Creek’s social media channels.
The most important news is the continued safety and health of all residents and team members. Thanks to a rigorous testing and safety regimen, to
date, Acacia Creek has experienced only 13 cases of COVID-19 among residents
and 17 among team members, with zero hospitalizations or deaths, out of 273
residents and team members. The board is conﬁdent that Acacia Creek will
remain a safe and healthy environment for everyone, even as the pandemic
continues to pose a serious threat. That’s a sentiment that’s been shared by
many residents and team members, who time and time again have expressed
their belief that Acacia Creek was the best possible place to be during such a
chaotic and frightening time.
Acacia Creek’s commitment to providing a safe and supportive atmosphere
was once again reﬂected in its annual resident survey. In 2022, 93 percent of
residents indicated their overall satisfaction with life on campus. Acacia Creek
residents demonstrate, through the annual Successful Aging Personal Review,
that they enjoy better health, nutrition, and physical activity than do those at
comparable communities elsewhere in the country, or even in their own homes
prior to moving to Acacia Creek.
Thanks to numbers like those, Acacia Creek remains certiﬁed as a Center
for Successful Aging—one of just 15 communities nationwide to earn that
designation, and the only one in Northern California. That certiﬁcation is
awarded to communities that have, over a ﬁve-year period, demonstrated a
culture where residents can continue to grow and thrive. This has been achieved
through the leadership’s commitment to providing opportunities for advanced
programming involving the physical, spiritual, social, and intellectual growth of
residents—the anchor of the Successful Aging philosophy. Acacia Creek’s partnership with Masterpiece LLC, a national organization which provides Acacia
Creek with education and programs on physical and mental wellness, remains
an important part of that success. Through Masterpiece LLC programs, Acacia
Creek residents and staﬀ members are empowered to pursue new skills, physical
activities, and opportunities for personal fulﬁllment, and to contribute to the
wider community. Since 2019, the Acacia Creek leadership team has focused
on training all team members and their families on Successful Aging goals to
encourage healthy living and promote job satisfaction. This includes opportunities for continuing education through a sponsored scholarship program.
Supporting team members in their own personal development is more
important than ever, particularly against a backdrop of staﬃng shortages across
the industry. (Nineteen percent of senior living communities reported severe
staﬃng shortages as of spring 2022, while nearly 75 percent had at least “moderate” shortages.) That’s why it’s important that Acacia Creek continues to follow
a team management concept and report a positive work environment. In the
2022 team member Satisfaction Survey, Acacia Creek team members rated their
work experience at a 95 percent satisfaction level. Acacia Creek has historically
enjoyed an industry-low 12 percent turnover ratio. Reliable team members play

194

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

a vital role in making the community an ideal place to live.
Another important milestone in Acacia Creek’s development came with
the opening of the Masonic Homes of California’s new Pavilion at the Masonic
Homes in the fall of 2021. Access to this new facility is an important differentiator for Acacia Creek. Through the Pavilion and our partnership with Masonic
Homes, residents at Acacia Creek can access highly skilled nursing and memory
care services just steps away. These offerings bring peace of mind to those who
may worry about aging in place, or about being separated from a loved one.
With the Pavilion at the Masonic Homes now open and available to residents
of Acacia Creek, those concerns can be put to rest.
The Board wishes to extend its sincere and continued appreciation to Bro.
Chuck Major, president of Acacia Creek, and Bro. Martin Herter, vice president
and administrator, who have maintained a high level of morale and accountability of the team during the pandemic. Together, they helped maintain the
high-quality lifestyle for the residents that is the vision and goal of Acacia Creek.
The board would further like to thank the members of the Grand Lodge
Executive Committee, the Grand Lodge staff, and the Masonic Homes Board
of Trustees. We are excited about our future, and together we look forward
to ensuring the continued success in support of the mission of Acacia Creek.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF THE
BOARD OF TRUSTEES
California Masonic Foundation
As Masons returned to lodge in 2022, they sent a clear statement:
Although much around them has changed, their commitment to the fraternity’s
charitable values has not.
In all, California Masons gave more than $8 million in 2022 toward the
fraternity’s charitable mission, including support of the Masonic Homes, public
education initiatives, and other philanthropic causes. That includes record-high
donations to Masons4Mitts, during which the program surpassed an important
milestone, as well as an outpouring of generosity shown in the wake of the crisis
in Ukraine. In all, it has been a highly successful year.
The California Masonic Foundation, led by its board of trustees and professional staff, has continued to fulfill its mission of ensuring that each California
Mason has the opportunity to act on his charitable impulse, and to help direct
that philanthropy to programs that enhance and support our fraternity. In 2022,
that included a wide range of campaigns, including the ongoing Distressed
Worthy Brother Relief Fund, which supports the Masonic Homes and brothers
at every stage of life, and a series of college-access and college-readiness programs including the literacy nonprofit Raising A Reader.
Throughout this successful fundraising, the Foundation also made important progress
in 2022 on other organizational priorities, particularly in identifying committed volunteer leaders. The impact that Masons make on the communities
around them is only as strong
as the individual leaders behind those efforts. That’s why it’s imperative
that the Foundation identifies members who can be effective leaders of key programs, such as chairing a Public Education Advisory Committee or serving as a
team captain for Masons4Mitts. Where we have strong leaders, we have success.
At the same time, the Foundation recognizes that leadership takes many
forms. For some, leadership can be shown through personal charity; for another,
it’s volunteering their time and energy. Others can help encourage those around
them to speak with pride about the Foundation’s mission and programs. All
of these leaders are critical to the success of not only the California Masonic
Foundation, but to the fraternity at large. It’s the Foundation’s intention to

196

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

197

continue to seek out these leaders and celebrate their contributions.
In 2022, California Masons demonstrated this kind of leadership through
their generosity. Over the past year, members gave to the Foundation at a higher
average gift level than in any year in the Foundation’s history. The average
member donation now stands at a record $311, reﬂecting a long-running trend
toward more impactful gifts and bringing the Foundation in line with other top
nonproﬁts and charities. The past year also saw an increase in overall member
giving, lodge oﬃcer giving, and recurring online gifts. Both Grand Master Circlelevel and Anniversary-level donors were both up in 2022. Simply put, Masons
are becoming more generous than ever. And thanks to our charitable programs,
that generosity is being put into action like never before.
While the Annual Fund underpins the Foundation’s critical work with the
Masonic Homes and in support of public schools, it’s the planned giving program
that generates the greatest single source of revenue for its charitable eﬀorts.
Members who include Masonic charities in their estate plans make the most
signiﬁcant contributions of all to the Foundation’s ability to fulﬁll its obligation
to provide relief for those in need.
In 2022, Masons have made planned gifts approaching $7 million in the
form of gifts from wills and trusts. These planned gifts are the bedrock of the
fraternity’s charitable programs. To each and every member who has made this
important decision, the Foundation thanks you. Your generosity is the key to
our future success.
These Masons are members of the Foundation’s Cornerstone Society, and
serve as important examples of Masonic leadership, inspiring others to give and
putting their hands up for others to see. It is the hope of the board that in 2023,
even more Masons will join the nearly 200 living members of the Cornerstone
Society who have made this powerful statement about their values and priorities.
Another important statement was sent this summer at Oracle Park in San
Francisco. Thanks to years of guidance by members like Rich Modolo, Kendall
Mills, Rod Moreland, and John Bermudez, the Northern California region of the
Foundation’s Masons4Mitts program surpassed $1 million in lifetime support
of the Junior Giants program and the Giants Community Fund. As our firstever Masons4Mitts foundation partner, the Giants Community Fund and the
California Masonic Foundation have forged an important working relationship.
Now, 14 years after first launching Masons4Mitts, our members were able
to celebrate that important milestone with a special pregame ceremony and
on-field check presentation.
The $1 million figure is particularly important. It represents more than
50,000 baseball gloves that have been distributed to Junior Giants players who
might otherwise have not had access to the program, which teaches not only
the skills of the game, but also important lessons about teamwork, character,
and sportsmanship. In recent years, the program has grown to incorporate
lessons on nutrition, fitness, and other important themes. For 50,000 young
people, the square and compass embossed into their own leather baseball

mitt is a reminder that someone they will likely never meet cared about their
happiness and growth.
In addition to the Giants Community Fund, Masons4Mitts continues to
partner with the charitable foundations of the Los Angeles Dodgers, Los Angeles
Angels, and San Diego Padres. In all, the program is approaching $1.8 million in
total gifts for the four programs. In each case, this support is about more than
baseball—and more than mitts. It’s about helping kids access important life
lessons and have the enriching summer experience we all know they deserve.
The Foundation’s other close charitable partnership continues to be a
strong one, as well. Since 2011, the Foundation and Raising A Reader have
worked together in support of family literacy by placing age-appropriate and
expert-vetted reading material into more than 800 of the state’s most under-resourced public school classrooms. By providing enriching and relevant books,
Raising A Reader has a demonstrated ability to help raise the rates of household
reading, and to foster in students a lifelong love of reading. Over the past 11
years, California Masons have donated more than $3.5 million to the program,
which plans to expand to beyond 1,000 classrooms within the coming years.
California Masons can take great pride in knowing that children and families
throughout our state are taking steps to break generational cycles of illiteracy.
We are truly making a difference.
The Foundation also remains committed to providing support to high
school graduates and college students through its many scholarship programs.
The C.E. Towne Masonic Awards support two primary groups of scholars. One
is our partnership with Prince Hall Masons, through which dozens of children
and grandchildren of Prince Hall Masons are able to receive an annual award
based on academic and financial need. The other is through the Masonic Youth
Leadership Award, which ensures that leaders of the Masonic youth orders
receive support for their higher educational goals. In addition to those awards,
the Foundation also supports the Investment in Success scholarship program.
Through Investment in Success, the Foundation partners with college-access and college-success organizations to help create a pathway to success for
first-generation college students. These are young people who may not have
the academic credentials of other students, but who have overcome significant
life obstacles and demonstrated great drive and character.
Lastly, the Working Tools scholarship is now in its second year, following
a pilot year which involved a great deal of learning. Through the Working Tools
program, students are able to access living-wage jobs through vocational education. COVID-19 presented difficulties for this program in particular, as training in
the trades and technical fields depends on hands-on, in-person learning. Despite
those challenges, the Foundation believes that California Masons can and will
support a program that demonstrates that the path to success post-high-school
includes more options than simply a four-year college degree.
The Foundation plans to make this one of its focal points over the next
two years. Working Tools will help promote well-paying jobs in the trades and

198

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

technical fields and encourage a new generation of students to investigate these
career options.
Overall, 2022 was a year of success for the California Masonic Foundation.
But it was also a time of sorrow and reflection, as Most Worshipful John R.
Heisner passed away. Most Worshipful Heisner was grand master in 2016–17, as
well as chairman of the California Masonic Foundation. Beyond that, he was a
leader in the fraternity and a strong proponent of public education. Our hearts
were heavy as we mourned our loss. Most Worshipful Heisner’s contributions to
our work are difficult to measure. California Freemasons everywhere will miss
his passion for the craft, his steady guidance, and his friendship and leadership.
The trustees would like to formally thank the staff of the California Masonic
Foundation, led by its president, Douglas Ismail. The Foundation’s staff, including Denise Avila, Candler Gibson, Greg Cherry, Joshua Castro, and Rich Kellogg,
have a combined experience with our fraternity exceeding 75 years. Their work
on behalf of the Foundation has been critical to its success—and we would like
to express our gratitude for their hard work.
We see 2023 as a time in which new leaders will step forward and carve their
own paths. New Public Education Advisory Committee chairs and members,
as well as new captains for Masons4Mitts, are already making their case to be
the drivers of our future. The success of the Foundation flows from its leaders.
Thank you for all your support of our efforts. Please consider joining our team
by being a donor or volunteer. We promise you will feel better for it.
Respectfully submitted,
Michael D. Thibodeaux, Chairman
Mark J. McNee, Vice Chairman
Douglas D. Ismail, President

REPORT OF THE
BOARD OF TRUSTEES
California Masonic Memorial Temple
After more than 18 months during which the California Masonic Memorial
Temple had essentially gone dark, 2021–22 saw a welcome return to in-person gatherings. That was never more in evidence than at last fall’s Annual
Communication, one of the first large-scale events to return to the building—
and a dramatic reminder of just how important it is to be back together again.
That return to something closer to business-as-usual defined the past year
at the California Masonic Memorial Temple. With Live Nation resuming a full
calendar of concerts and events, Freemasons’ Hall hosting a full complement
of lodge meetings, and much of the staff of the Grand Lodge returning to the
office, the building had its typical buzz of activity.
Financially, the CMMT is nearly back to pre-pandemic revenue levels, and
the Board is working to catch up on its 10-Year Capital Plan for improvements,
some aspects of which were delayed over the past two years. As before, all
improvements are paid for through the CMMT’s operating cash flow. Through
the consolidation of certain leases and renegotiation of new contracts, the
Board anticipates revenue from the CMMT rooftop communications system
to increase this year to approximately $100,000 annually. All told, the board
anticipates a positive cashflow for CMMT of approximately $733,000 this year.
The CMMT also plays an important role to the wider fraternity. Net revenue
generated through the building supports the efforts of the California Masonic
Foundation. And as part of the 2025 Fraternity Plan, the Board has adopted
a plan to activate the building and its various meeting spaces to support the
fraternity’s goal of improving positive awareness. To that end, visitors now
encounter several QR codes placed around, within, and outside the building,
which direct them toward information about the history of the building and
California Freemasonry generally. (That effort coincides with a dedicated issue
of California Freemason Magazine devoted to telling the story of the California
Masonic Memorial Temple.) This, along with new online content about the
CMMT and its importance to the fraternity, should help generate interest in
Freemasonry among some of the 250,000-plus visitors to the building each year.

REPORT OF THE
BOARD OF TRUSTEES
Nob Hill Masonic Center
The past year has been an important one for the Nob Hill Masonic Center.
After working hard to initially weather the storm brought on by the pandemic,
the NHMC in fiscal year 2022 has pivoted its operations and brought in new
revenue streams to remain profitable. As the Grand Lodge of California’s only
for-profit entity, it is responsible for ensuring the efficient and effective operation of the California Masonic Memorial Temple garage in order to generate
an annual dividend for the Grand Lodge, which is its sole stockholder.
In 2020, the pandemic significantly disrupted the NHMC business model.
Since March 2020, the fiscal impact of the pandemic to the garage is in excess
of $761,000 in lost net profits. Almost overnight, daily and special-event parking
receipts evaporated, and monthly parking suffered as neighborhood residents
moved away or temporarily relocated. That spring, the NHMC board developed
a three-part recovery plan to address the loss in revenue. Thanks to that plan,
along with reserves generated in previous years, the NHMC was able to make
its annual dividend payment of $350,000 in 2021 and expects to make its dividend payment for 2022.
Two significant changes have contributed to success in 2022: Revenue
from monthly and event parking has rebounded strongly, and the operation
of the Grace Cathedral Parking Lot, which began January 1, has contributed to
increased profits. Midway through FY2022, overall net profits were $319,267—
more than $200,000 better than originally planned for. The end result is that
the garage is now posting slightly better than pre-pandemic revenues, despite
the fact that some pandemic-era effects continue to be felt.
Event parking has seen a sharp increase in 2022, with Live Nation having
resumed its typical schedule of concerts. Since its first concert, in August 2021,
the promoter has returned to its full calendar of 79 yearly events and brought
with it a dramatic increase in special-event parking receipts. Year-to-date, event
parking is very nearly back to pre-pandemic levels.
Meanwhile, monthly parking has not only recovered, but set and broken
records for quarterly revenue. With an average of 351 monthly parkers in 2022,
the garage grossed more than $400,000 in the first quarter of the fiscal year,
best in its history. Though daily parking continues to lag in its recovery (down

202

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

45 percent compared to pre-pandemic figures), the strength of monthly parking
contracts and the return of special-event parking mean that the garage’s core
offerings are close to 2019 levels.
The NHMC has also activated a significant new revenue stream with the
management of the Grace Cathedral Parking Garage. The board began leasing
and operating the garage, located across California Street at 1051 Taylor Street,
on January 1, 2022. By March of 2022, operations at the Grace Cathedral Garage
were profitable. At the end of the second fiscal quarter, gross revenues from
Grace Cathedral stood at $168,024—enough to push overall revenues above 2019
levels. The management of the Grace Cathedral garage is expected to contribute
to a much-improved financial picture for NHMC by the end of fiscal year 2022.
Several improvements at the Nob Hill garage are ongoing. The new PARCS
system, or Parking Access and Revenue Control System, was installed in early
2022, and now provides more detailed management of ticketing and receipts. In
fact, in July, the PARCS replacement project was selected by the International
Parking and Mobility Institute to be the subject of a presentation at its annual
conference, which was dedicated to ways parking garage owners were able to
take advantage of the pandemic to modernize technology. A new license plate
recognition system is also being installed in September to provide further
control over parking operations.
NHMC installed two DCFC supercharging stations and two additional
Level 2 electric-car chargers this year. The move is being made to comply with
a San Francisco city ordinance requiring garages to include a certain number
of electric-vehicle charging stations. In June, the NHMC signed an agreement
with the charging company Volta, under which Volta will lease the space for the
four chargers and pay their electrical expenses. Volta installed the equipment
at no charge to NHMC, as its business model is instead based on ad sales.
Another major improvement involves updating the signage at the entrance
to the garage. This year, the board began working with an environmental design
firm to review the garage’s overall signage, wayfinding, and visual identity, with
an aim to ultimately introduce clearer, more visually pleasing and useful signage.
The first two phases of that five-part plan, which center on reviewing existing
signage, are underway.
The Nob Hill Masonic Center Board’s relationship with the wider community remains a priority. Relations have historically been strong, and continue to
be so. As a member of the Nob Hill Liaison Group and the Nob Hill Association,
the NHMC is a respected voice in the community. NHMC President and Chief
Executive Allan Casalou was elected to serve as president and board chair of the
Nob Hill Association, which is planning to continue its annual Holiday Lighting
Ceremony in Huntington Park this year on November 28.
The Board wishes to extend its appreciation to its president and chief
executive, Grand Secretary Allan Casalou, and to all the management and staff
of the Grand Lodge who support its business. In addition, it thanks the grand
master, Most Worshipful Jeffery M. Wilkins, and the executive committee for

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

their confidence and support.

REPORT OF THE
COMMITTEE ON INSURANCE
The Masons of California’s corporate insurance program provides
coverage for lodges, hall associations, the Masonic Homes of California, Acacia
Creek, and the California Masonic Memorial Temple (CMMT and Nob Hill
Masonic Center. The program includes coverage for property, general liability,
umbrella liability, earthquake, D-and-O, employment practices liability, and
crime insurance policies, all of which were renewed on April 1, 2022.
We continue as we ended last year’s insurance program, with a tough renewal.
By now we are all aware of the pressures on the insurance industry with respect
to insurers’ appetite for fire exposures. The result is a reduced capacity to provide adequate limits and an overall increase in rates. Put simply, fire losses are
driving rate increases. On a positive note, our fire insurer has held deductibles
at the same level for the past three years. With the onset of COVID-19, insurers
across the industry have added communicable disease exclusions. The specific
exclusion of COVID-19-related losses is not unexpected. As was done the past
three years, our insurance broker, Marsh, conducted a full insurance market
review. Grand Lodge staff and the Insurance Committee worked diligently to look
at cost-saving areas as well as ideas beyond traditional insurance transactions.
These included self-insurance, insurance captives, and other risk-transfer methods. The committee will continue to review alternative risk-transfer methods.
Marsh reached out early to insurance markets and wholesale brokers. The
result is a 9 percent increase, on top of a 9.3 percent increase last year. Marsh
navigated a difficult marketplace, but we are confident that we have identified the
most favorable coverages available to us. All premiums noted below are before
taxes and fees, if applicable. All policy deductibles noted below are per claim.

Conclusions
The property program premium continues to drive the overall program costs
upward. We don’t see an end to the trend as long as there is a 12-month fire
season in California. Grand Lodge staff and the committee continue to push
hall owners for reviews and increases in values where possible. The Insurance
Committee cannot stress enough that this is not a one-year occurrence. Hall
management should continue to focus on deferred maintenance issues and
start preventative maintenance programs immediately.
Overall, the program was renewed in what continues to be a difficult market.
Insurers are facing huge losses from climate change, fires, hurricanes, and flooding, and these are becoming more frequent and severe. We see no changes in
this trend. In addition, cyber-related losses are now on insurers’ radar. Overall,
we pushed our broker to persuade underwriters to provide the best terms possible. In addition, as noted, work must continue with halls to help them better
understand the need to provide realistic replacement cost values and understand
that good housekeeping directly relates to ensuring broad coverage and reduced
premiums. Terrorism coverage is purchased on all the major lines of insurance.

REPORT OF THE
COMMITTEE ON INVESTMENT
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

Overview
The Investment Committee has been charged with the prudent handling
of Grand Lodge investment funds. These funds consist primarily of the General
and Endowment funds for the Masonic Homes of California, but also include
the investment portfolios of the California Masonic Foundation, California
Masonic Memorial Temple and the Grand Lodge itself.
The financial objectives for these funds are laid out in our approved
Investment Policy Statement:
The primary objectives of the funds are to provide a regular and reliable
source of financial support to the Masonic entity or its beneficiaries, while
preserving the purchasing power of the funds after withdrawals are taken.
In plain English, we are tasked to make sure that the Homes, the Foundation
and all entities that are entrusting their funds to our care can expect to receive
a reasonable income, while their principle keeps pace with expected inflation
over time.
As a simple example, if one of the entities wanted to be able to rely on a 4.5
percent distribution from its money, we know we’d have to earn at least that,
by investing. If we also expected inflation to be 2 percent per year on average
(eroding purchasing power of the principal), we’d know that we also want to
grow the principle by 2 percent per year on average. We’d then know that we
needed to build a portfolio that could reasonably be expected to return 6.5
percent over the long-term (4.5 percent spending + 2 percent inflation).
This example, while simple, is actually very close to the actual numbers
used to form our return goals for the Grand Lodge investments.
The job of the Committee, then, is to build the portfolio with the best
chance of accomplishing that return goal over the long-term, while exposing
the portfolio to the least risk needed to attain that goal.
While the committee is comprised of diligent financial professionals who
are astute in portfolio construction and global economics themselves; we also

Grand Lodge & Related Entity Investment Performance
for the year ended June 30, 2022:
The Total Grand Lodge and Related Entities portfolio earned a rate of return of
-10.7 percent for the year ending June 30, 2022. The relevant period consisted of
both a tremendous growth period during calendar year 2021, as well as a sharp
and sustained drop due to inflation and the interest rate increases designed to
fight it, primarily, in 2022. The total fund policy benchmark during the same
period was down 12.8 percent. The market value of the Total Grand Lodge and
Related Entities portfolio as of June 30, 2022 was $972,985,730. For the three-year
period ending June 30, 2022, the combined Grand Lodge and Related Entities
portfolio returned an average return of 5.4 percent versus 4.6 percent for the
benchmark. Since inception, our funds have returned 7.3 percent annually versus
7.3 percent return of the benchmark.

financial objectives of the funds.

Year in Review Activity
Allocation Changes:
This year we slightly reduced our exposure to real assets and private debt,
and added to our US equity, non-US equity and fixed income.
Investment Managers Hired:
We believe that a disciplined manager selection process will result in a
higher probability of hiring superior managers. We believe that past performance
is an unreliable predictor of future success and is only one of many factors that
should be used in the selection process.
During this period, the managers hired were:
• Emerging Markets Equity
• IShares MSCI Emerging Markets ETF
• Private Real Estate/ Real Assets
• Vision Ridge Sustainable Assets Fund
• Private Equity
• Spark Capital
• Thoma Bravo
Investment Managers Terminated:
Once managers have been thoroughly vetted and consistently monitored,
as long as the manager’s investment style is still part of our overall investment
thesis, it is relatively rare that a manager get terminated, unless we have adjusted
the positioning of the portfolio. In the last three years, we have, indeed, made
several positioning changes. Much of the change comes from our positive effort
to create a Private Markets portion of the portfolio.
As part of our fundamental philosophy, stated in our investment policy
statement:
“We believe that manager turnover is very expensive and extremely disruptive
to the efficient and productive operation of an investment program. Managers

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

217

should be hired with a long-run view… We also believe that constant and/or
rapid turnover of managers, justified solely on the basis of relative underperformance is usually an indication of a lack of adherence to the selection
and retention process. In particular, short-term (generally less than one
year) underperformance should not be a reason for termination, unless it
is accompanied by other adverse key retention characteristics.”
During this period, the managers terminated were:
• Emerging Markets Equity
• Allianz Emerging Markets
Grand Lodge Investment Management
In order to fulfill our responsibilities in accordance with the Grand Lodge
investment policy and philosophy, the investment committee meets quarterly
with our investment consultant, NEPC, LLC. We also meet with our individual
portfolio managers as needed and review due diligence reports quarterly from
the consultants. We monitor the respective performance of the managers compared to various indices representing their objective. This process provides the
Investment Committee with the necessary data to evaluate each investment
manager on a timely basis, and to observe whether they continue to achieve
the objectives of their mandate.
The committee also holds ad-hoc conference calls (as needed) to discuss
any outstanding business or discuss the implementation of tactical changes
within the portfolio.
Your Grand Lodge Investment Committee is also available to assist individual lodges in determining appropriate investment strategies. We are also here
to help lodges establish a set of policies and procedures that are designed to
ensure assets are invested according to the needs of the lodge and to safeguard
against the misuse of funds. Investment Committee members continue to make
themselves available to the lodges for assistance with this program and other
questions regarding lodge investments.
Summary
I am honored to present this report on behalf of the Investment Committee
of the Grand Lodge of California. It continues to work with much fervency and
zeal to ensure that your assets are properly stewarded, and I am glad to have
their efforts and dedication. I want to thank Russell Godt for his tremendous
service to the craft and the committee during his tenure. Thank you for allowing
me to serve as Chair this year, it is both an honor and a privilege to work with
all the gentlemen on the committee.

Proposed Recommendations and Resolutions

REPORT OF THE
COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The committee on jurisprudence serves as the legal adviser to the grand
master and the legal adviser to the Grand Lodge when in session. The committee
reviews proposed resolutions and recommendations to be considered at the
next Annual Communication and prepares any necessary legislation to carry
out the intent of the proponents. At the Annual Communication, it comments
on the legality of the grand master’s decisions and dispensations, and on the
legal effect of the proposed recommendations and resolutions. After the Annual
Communication, it prepares the changes to the California Masonic Code to reflect
the legislation which was adopted.

Grand Master Wilkins’s
Decisions and Dispensations
In the committee’s view, those of Grand Master Wilkins’s decisions and dispensations coming to its attention were legal and within his discretion.
On October 14, 2021, Grand Master Wilkins issued a decision entitled
“Resumption of In-Person Meetings; No Further Virtual Stated Meetings.” In
that decision, Grand Master Wilkins noted that Past Grand Master Weiss’s
directive implementing the virtual meeting provisions of CMC §§807.000 and
807.010 expired at the close of the 2021 Annual Communication. The Grand
Master also noted that the California Department of Public Health had lifted its
Covid-related prohibitions on in-person meetings and that counties and cities
throughout California had likewise lifted similar prohibitions on in-person meetings. Accordingly, the grand master found no cause or justification to renew Past
Grand Master Weiss’s directives related to virtual meetings. As Past Grand Master
Weiss’s directives had expired, and as the implementation of the virtual meeting provisions of CMC §807.010 is subject to the grand master’s determination
that assembling the required number of persons for holding a special meeting is
prohibited by competent local, state, or national authority, it is the committee’s
view that Grand Master Wilkins’s decision was legal and within his discretion.

In the committee’s view, the legislation posted by the grand secretary to the
Grand Lodge website on August 9 of this year is sufficient to carry out the intent
of the proponents. We believe that each piece of this legislation has the legal
effect set forth in it.
In presenting the legislation for your consideration, we make no recommendations as to the action to be taken with it. While the committee has written the
title and introductory explanation for each resolution before you and assisted
the proponents in drafting the code changes required to effect their intent, the
proponents’ arguments in their whereas clauses are their own. The committee
does not assist in drafting the whereas clauses and makes no comments on them.
The legislation posted by the grand secretary to the Grand Lodge website on
August 9 of this year requires no separate motion because they are automatically
before this Annual Communication. The presiding officer will announce the vote
required for the passage of each item before discussion begins. Any legislation
which does not amend the California Masonic Code or the ritual requires a simple
majority only for adoption. Any amendment to the California Masonic Code or
the ritual must be adopted by a five-sixths affirmative vote. If the amendment
receives a simple majority but less than a five-sixths affirmative vote, it carries
over to the next Annual Communication, when only a two-thirds affirmative
vote is required for adoption.
Committee Actions on Unmasonic Conduct
In addition to the foregoing responsibilities, the committee also reviews all
charges of unmasonic conduct, strikes out those portions which are not supported by a clear and precise specification of unmasonic conduct, and revises
those portions which are incorrect, ambiguous, or insufficient. As part of its
review, the committee provides the parties with every essential factual element
which must be proven at trial for the accused to be found guilty of each charge.
The committee may dismiss charges if all the facts set forth in the specifications, even if true, would not warrant a verdict of unmasonic conduct. If in the
committee’s judgment a dispute warrants pre-trial mediation, the grand master
may at his discretion appoint one or more Master Masons to mediate any such
dispute. Since the last Annual Communication, the committee commented on
the charges and specifications in 12 trials.
If a Mason under the disciplinary jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge has
pleaded guilty or nolo contendere (or no contest) to, or has been convicted
of, a crime of moral turpitude by a federal or state court, he shall be deemed
automatically expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry without
any further action of his lodge or grand lodge. The committee reviews a certified copy of the record of conviction to determine whether there has been an
automatic expulsion. Since the last Annual Communication, the committee
has reviewed one federal or state court record to evaluate whether there has

234

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

been an automatic expulsion of the Mason involved in the proceeding. These
matters are summarized in the attached Exhibit A.
No person shall hold or be eligible for membership in any constituent
lodge who has pleaded guilty or nolo contendere to, or has been convicted of, a
crime involving a violation of the moral law unless, for the reason that he did
not commit the offense, he either has been pardoned or had his judgment of
conviction vacated or reversed. All applicants are subject to background checks
to determine compliance with this rule. Since the last Annual Communication,
the grand secretary has asked the committee to review one federal or state court
record to evaluate whether an applicant is eligible for the degrees.
We thank the grand master for the opportunity which he has given us to
serve this year.

Exhibit A

Respectfully submitted,
David M. Ferreria, Chairman
R. Stephen Doan, P.G.M., Vice Chairman
Michael H. Anatole
Vance Thomas Langford
David L. Brandon

Trial No. 2994
In Trial No. 2994, the member pled guilty to a violation of California Penal
Code Section 530.5(A) (the “Crime”). This section provides that any person who
“willfully obtains personal identifying information…of another person and uses
that information for any unlawful purpose…without consent of that person, is
guilty of a public offense” and subject to a fine and/or imprisonment pursuant to
subdivision (h) of Section 1170. Section 100.075 of the California Masonic Code
and 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No. 2 provide guidance as to the meaning of
the term of moral turpitude. For conduct to involve moral turpitude, it normally
must be accompanied by an inherently evil intent. An inherently evil intent is
not required for a conviction under Section 530.5(A) of the California Penal
Code. Automatic expulsion is not appropriate unless the only activity for which
there could have been a conviction under the applicable statute involves moral
turpitude. Therefore, based on the court record and the foregoing analysis, it is
the judgment of a majority of the members of the committee on jurisprudence
that the member had not pled guilty to, pled no contest to, nor been convicted
of a crime of moral turpitude before a federal or state court.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON MASONIC PROPERTIES
Good afternoon, Most Worshipful Sir and brethren,
On behalf of your Masonic properties committee, we urge a “no”
vote on this resolution.
Despite not increasing the threshold of $25,000 over the last 22 years, the
committee on Masonic properties does not feel that in itself is justification to
pass this resolution.
Adopting this resolution will not decrease the burden of hall associations,
since they still need to gather the same information we require for review,
regardless of the threshold amount.
Over the past 5 years, our committee reviewed a total of 45 applications under
$100,000. Of which only 22 were under $50,000. That makes it less than five per
year. Once our committee receives all the necessary documents, it submits its
recommendations to the hall association, and forward its recommendations to
the Executive Committee if the contract is above $100,000, within 10 days or less.
Any delays in approval is a result of a hall association not providing all the necessary documents for review up front. We require only the documents necessary
to ensure existence of a valid contract and insurance, while avoiding unnecessary
risk and further liabilities. If a hall association does not have these documents
readily available, then they are already in danger of a negative outcome.
Our committee does not believe that an increase in the threshold will
impact the amount of applications submitted to the committee on an annual
basis. However, increasing the threshold will allow hall associations and lodges
to circumvent the requirement for proper review.
The committee consists of well experienced Brethren from different professional backgrounds pertaining and applicable to the maintenance of buildings, construction, engineering, contracting, project management, real estate,
and financial analysis. Together we are able to submit recommendations that
protected applicants from the following:
• Erroneous contracts. We have reviewed contracts that were written and
found to be incomplete after they were chosen by the respective hall
boards, we were not sure if the contractors wrote them intentionally
in a way, so that they would be able to charge the Hall Association for
contingencies and change orders, intentionally raising the costs.

• Contracts that did not include proper permits, which could be detrimental to lodges with very minimal assets. For example, if damage is
done to the building by a contractor who did not obtain a proper permit
before commencing the work, the insurance company may not be willing to cover the cost of the damages. Leaving the liability on the lodge.
• Hall associations or lodges entering into a contract where they would
likely be spending more money than they have available in their
investments. Our committee reviews the financial standing of the
lodge to ensure adequate funding to complete their projects, including potential unforeseen additional costs.
The brothers of your committee give the hall association board members
“free advice” I repeat, “free advice”.
These recommendations have saved hall association and lodges, including
personal liability of the board directors, a lot of risk and money.
Brethren, please be reminded that the funds involved in these projects were
generational and from the hard work of all our brethren from ages of contributions to our lodges, and we have to be the best stewards of these funds for the
benefit of our future generations.
If for all intents and purposes; hall association should be encouraged to use
the free services of the Masonic Properties Committee for their expertise and
experience, and not consider it cumbersome, but a valuable asset.
Most Worshipful, on behalf of Worshipful Lawrence Hopper, Chairman and
the rest of the members of the Masonic Properties Committee, I would like
to thank you for your confidence and allowing us to be of service to our craft.
Brethren, I appeal to you to vote accordingly for this resolution.

REPORT OF THE
COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATIVE ANALYSIS

Recommendation No. 1

Decision No.1
This decision would clarify the use of the title of past master when a lodge’s
charter is suspended and the master is removed from office.
California Masonic Code section 805.020 states the title of past master
applies only to a member who: (A) Has been regularly elected or named in a
charter as master of a chartered lodge; (B) Has been installed as master of a
chartered lodge; (C) Has served until the installation of his successor, except
in the case of death or consolidation as specified, or has served until reinstalled
as master for the subsequent year; and (D) Is at the time in good standing.
Recently, some confusion has arisen as to whether the title of past master
applies to a member who was elected and installed as master of a chartered
lodge, but who did not install a successor because the lodge’s charter was suspended and he was removed as master. Had he remained in office when the
charter was returned, and had he installed his successor, he would have earned
the title of past master. This decision would resolve that confusion by more
clearly stating that the title of past master does not apply in that situation.
Resolution 22-02 competes with this decision, as it would authorize the
grand master to confer the title of past master in that situation. As this is a
decision and not a recommendation, it is not binding on succeeding grand
masters. Decisions are recorded simply to preserve for future reference what
the Grand Lodge has on a prior occasion determined to be permissible application of our current law.
Clearly, when a lodge’s charter is suspended, and the master is removed
from office before the charter is returned or the charter is revoked, did not
install his successor, and did not complete his term of office, he should not be
afforded the title of past master.
This decision provides the clarification that he is not a past master.
If both Resolution 22-02 and this decision pass, then this decision would
be moot, as the code will have been updated by 22-02.

This recommendation would amend the California Masonic Code section
807.000 to create greater flexibility for lodges that desire to meet at least
quarterly to satisfy their constitutional requirements, while allowing them
to meet their administrative burdens at the meeting specified in their bylaws
immediately following the currently mandated February and August meetings.
The Annual Election of Officers will be required in one of the stated meetings
in the fourth quarter. If a lodge chooses to meet more than once in the last
quarter of the calendar year, and one of those meetings is in November, then the
lodge shall hold elections in November. The duty to annually and semi-annually
report, and hold annual elections does not cease.
A lodge that currently decides to meet fewer than 12 times per year is
restricted in the months it may choose. A lodge that holds stated meetings only
once per quarter must meet in February for the Treasurer’s and Secretary’s
Annual Reports as required at sections 805.220(d) and 805.230(d). A lodge
must also meet in August for the Treasurer’s and Secretary’s Semi-Annual as
required by the same sections. A lodge must also meet in November for the
Annual Election of Officers as required in section 805.410.
This recommendation expands upon resolution 19-07 that allowed lodges
to set a minimum quarterly stated meeting schedule. That current requirement
could require lodges to meet more than quarterly to factor in the required
constitutional meetings of February, August, and November.
This recommendation does not apply to special meetings, and the lodge
would still be enabled to hold as many special meetings and non-tiled events as
its calendar and candidate flow would allow. It may be noted that in many jurisdictions, lodges go dark in summer months, or meet quarterly as well. Lodges
in areas that experience extremely high temperatures might choose to move
their require stated meetings to more comfortable and less-costly operating
months, and lodges with extraordinarily cold weather might move meetings
to months that are safer for their members’ participation.
This recommendation does not create a blanket requirement for all lodges
to amend their by-laws to alter their current meetings; lodges are already authorized to meet at a minimum of once a quarter. This resolution only creates an
option for lodges to meet their burdens in a manner which best serves a lodge’s
local condition.

Recommendation No. 2

Carryover Recommendation No. 3

This recommendation would require each lodge to have an executive committee. That committee would be composed of the master, wardens, treasurer,
and secretary of the lodge. And it would be required to meet some time prior
to every stated meeting.
This recommendation would amend the California Masonic Code, section
806.000 to add the executive committee to the list of standing committees that
each lodge is required to have. CMC section 806.000 governs lodge committees
and it currently requires only three standing committees: the charity committee,
the auditing committee, and the member retention committee. It also authorizes
the lodge or master to form any other committee they deem proper.
Protecting lodge autonomy has been important to this Grand Lodge since
its formation. Some practices are beneficial for some lodges, and not others.
Mandating practices have typically arisen from legal requirements or a compelling reason. While there is no legal reason for requiring every lodge to have
an executive committee, there may be a compelling one.
The benefits of executive committees are well-established. The Lodge
Manual explains how the Grand Lodge executive committee works and then
explains how a lodge could and should create its own executive committee to
help build a consistent vision and sustained leadership over a multi-year period.
The Lodge Health Check, a resource published by the Grand Lodge, mentions
“executive committee” 32 times while touting the benefits and uses for such a
committee. And a “cohesive executive committee” is the first characteristic of
“strong lodges and halls” identified in the Long-Term Planning Guide.
By contrast, mandating executive committees should create a minimal
burden for those lodges that do not already have them. CMC section 805.210
already requires wardens to “assist the master in the performance of his duties.”
And the duties of secretaries and treasurers—as specified in CMC sections
805.220 and 805.230—already require them to work with each other and the
master.
The burdens of an executive committee are typically minimal. It is likely
that most members already expect the elected officers of their lodge to meet
regularly. And the meetings need not be in person; they can be done virtually
or over the phone.
It is for this voting body to decide whether the benefits of requiring every
lodge to have an executive committee outweigh the burdens and the resulting
infringement on lodge autonomy.

This recommendation seeks to give a lodge the option to make the business
portion of its stated meetings available for virtual participation.
Due to the Covid-19 pandemic, it became necessary to find ways for lodges
throughout the state to stay connected to their members as well as conduct
business. Virtual meetings through the use of Zoom and other similar technologies became the standard for business meetings throughout the nation.
Lodges started using virtual meetings to assemble together for social events
even before their use was authorized for stated meetings.
In 2020 and 2021, lodges held virtual stated meetings. The procedures and
limited scope of those meetings protected the confidentiality of sensitive matters. As l odges have returned to in-person meetings, some have expressed interest in maintaining the newfound accessibility that virtual meetings provided.
This recommendation would authorize a hybrid of a traditional in-person
stated meetings and a virtual meeting. In the lodge room, the brethren physically
present would be giving the due guard and sign of the first degree throughout
the meeting. Since it is impossible to effectively tile a virtual meeting, this recommendation would require the camera only be turned on during the reading of
the minutes, reports of investigating committees, balloting, reception of applications, and miscellaneous and unfinished business. Further, the camera would
be solely focused on the master, who never gives the due guard or sign during
these portions of business. This minimizes the chance for someone to inadvertently see the due guard and sign on camera. However, a lodge would need to
be careful to ensure that no other brother is shown on camera. Transmission
of any other portions of the meeting, including the opening and closing ritual
or election of officers, would not be permitted.
Only Masons of the lodge would be permitted to attend virtually. Members
of the lodge would be permitted to vote virtually on items that require a voice
vote or the raising of hands, but no virtual balloting would be permitted. Thus,
balloting on membership and affiliations would be limited to the members
attending in person. Quorum would still be determined by the number of
members attending in person. And any Mason participating virtually would
not be permitted to fill any lodge office, place, or station.
An issue inherent with virtual meetings is the potential for cowans and
eavesdroppers. While most of the business that would be permitted under this
recommendation is not confidential, the reading of an application for membership or affiliation includes personally identifiable information that is not

242

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

normally shared outside a tiled meeting. If this recommendation is adopted,
further guidance may be necessary to protect the privacy of applicants.
This recommendation would create an option, not a requirement, and
would affect only stated meetings.

Carryover Recommendation No. 4
The intent of this recommendation is to ensure that a brother accused of
unmasonic conduct is not subject to charges on the same facts at a later date
or “double jeopardy” if he is party to a mediated settlement agreement that
meets certain conditions. It does not change the mediation process under the
CMC. Under the current provisions of the CMC, double jeopardy protection
is not afforded to an accused that enters into a settlement agreement resulting
from any form of mediation. If this recommendation is approved, double jeopardy protection would be afforded to an accused that enters into a settlement
agreement at mediation subject to the following conditions:
1.

The settlement agreement is in writing signed by the accused, the
accuser(s) and the trial master,

2.

The settlement agreement includes a summary of the facts and reasoning supporting the withdrawal of the charges,

3.

The grand master has ordered that double jeopardy protection be
afforded, and

4.

The Committee on Trial Review has given its concurrence (which
includes reporting to and obtaining the approval of Grand Lodge at the
Annual Communication). This requirement to obtain your approval
is the intent of Grand Master Weiss and the legal opinion of the
Jurisprudence Committee.

Double jeopardy protection would not be afforded to any other mediated
settlement agreements, including settlement agreements reached by way of
a mediation prior to the appointment of a trial master. If double jeopardy
protection is afforded to a mediated settlement agreement, such protection
would make those agreements not only binding on the parties, but also a final
resolution on the charges such that no Mason (whether or not party to the settlement agreement) would thereafter be able to pursue charges of unmasonic
conduct on the same facts. The CMC already provides a means for an accused
to receive this form of double jeopardy protection when the dispute is settled
by way of a trial.

Carryover Recommendation No. 5
This recommendation would amend two sections of the California Masonic
Code to create the penalty of transfer of membership from the accused brother’s lodge(s) to the Grand Master’s Lodge to those penalties that a trial master
may choose from when an accused brother is found guilty of unmasonic conduct. Currently, voluntary demits are being used during mediations to resolve
conflicts in lodges.
There has not been any previous legislation before Grand Lodge that proposed the creation of this penalty. The penalty of transfer of membership
would be one of the lowest penalties available to the trial master, on a par with
reprimand in open lodge. The trial master would have to make a finding that
the brother’s continued membership in one or more lodges was not in the best
interest of the craft and set the penalty as transfer of membership. If the accused
belongs to more than one lodge and the trial master does not transfer all of his
memberships, then the accused would remain a member of those other lodges
and not be placed in the Grand Master’s Lodge. As with all trials, the finding of
guilt and the suitability of the penalty would have to be approved by the Grand
Lodge at an Annual Communication.
A brother who has his membership transferred to the Grand Master’s Lodge
would retain all of the rights and privileges of membership in California. The
recommendation does not speak to the issue of the transferred brother who
wants to visit the lodge from which he was removed. He would be a visitor and
CMC section 808.040 authorizes the master to deny entry. He would pay dues
to the Grand Master’s Lodge as long as he remains a member. It would be up

244

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

to him to find another regular lodge and apply for affiliation. He could even
apply to his former lodge for affiliation, but it would be subject to a ballot by
its members.
If this recommendation is adopted, the Committee on Trial Review will need
to develop guidelines and procedures for use by trial masters in determining
when to appropriately use the penalty of transferred membership.
It is for this voting body to decide whether this would add a useful tool to
the penalties available to a trial master after a finding of guilt.

Resolutions for 2022
Resolution 22-02
This resolution would authorize the grand master to confer the title of past
master upon a brother who served as master of his lodge but did not complete
his entire term because the lodge’s charter was suspended or revoked.
It would not require that the title of past master be conferred upon the
brother, but it would permit the grand master to investigate and contemplate
all of the circumstances of the situation and to consider the circumstances of
other similar situations in his consideration as to whether or not to confer the
past master title upon the brother.
The proponents assert that the suspension or revocation of a lodge’s charter might not be a reflection of the sitting master’s performance, and that he
may have served and performed admirably despite the lodge’s problems. They
contend that if the g rand master determines this is the case, then he should
have the authority to acknowledge the brother’s service by conferring the past
master title upon him.
California Masonic Code section 805.020 states the title of past master
applies only to a member who: (A) Has been regularly elected or named in a
charter as master of a chartered lodge; (B) Has been installed as master of a
chartered lodge; (C) Has served until the installation of his successor, except
in the case of death or consolidation as specified, or has served until reinstalled
as master for the subsequent year; and (D) Is at the time in good standing.
This resolution would amend CMC section 805.020 to give the grand master
the discretion to confer the title upon a brother who did not serve until the
installation of his successor because the lodge’s charter was suspended and he
was removed from office or the lodge’s charter was revoked.
This resolution would not impose any time limitations on the conferral
of the past master title by the grand master, nor would it limit the number
of times a request to confer the past master title could be submitted to
the grand master or succeeding grand masters. This would allow requests
to be made to grand masters several years down the road who may not be
familiar with the facts and circumstances at the time and after memories
have somewhat faded. Furthermore, it could result in a scenario wherein
successive grand masters, year after year, are lobbied to confer the past
master title upon the brother until some grand master eventually says yes.
Additionally, this resolution could disrupt the peace and harmony within a

246

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

lodge For example, the grand master might confer the past master title on a
brother when his lodge believes him undeserving, or vice versa. Additionally,
as the resolution is written, the grand master’s decision on whether or not to
confer the past master title would not be subject to the review or approval of
the Grand Lodge.
There are social and other benefits to being a past master. A past master
is eligible to cast the collective vote of the past masters of his lodge at Annual
Communication per CMC section 403.075. He continues to be addressed as
“Worshipful” after he completes his term. He may receive gifts, such as an
apron, a life membership, or some other honorarium from his lodge. It is entirely
understandable that a brother who diligently executed his duties as a lodge
master would want to be acknowledged as a past master for his service, even
if his lodge’s charter was revoked or suspended through no fault of his own.
Traditionally, if a master has been removed from office or the lodge’s charter
has been revoked before he completes his first term, he has not been entitled to
the title of past master. It is for this Grand Lodge to decide whether the benefits
afforded by this resolution to a master who would otherwise not qualify as a
past master should be adopted.
If both this resolution and Grand Master’s Decision No. 1 pass, then the
decision would be moot, as the CMC will have been updated by this resolution
and this resolution would then govern.

Resolution 22-03
This resolution would amend California Masonic Code section 811.010 to prohibit the serving, consumption, and sale of alcoholic beverages immediately
before or after a stated meeting or conferral of a degree, and immediately
before, during, or after the course of a degree practice. CMC section 811.010 also
governs the storage of alcohol, but this resolution does not amend that section.
The proponents of this resolution assert that:
a.

The consumption of alcohol is overshadowing lodge business and
degree importance.

b.

Too many members are consuming alcohol before, during, or after
their attendance at stated meetings and degrees.

c.

That candidates are engaged in drinking prior to degrees.

d.

Members are driving home impaired from alcohol consumption.

e.

And that a return to the integrity of our degrees and meetings is
in need.

The CMC requires the master of a lodge to see that his lodge is conducted
in peace and harmony and with sobriety. CMC section 804.815 authorizes a

Further delay may result if a Masonic hall association does not submit required
documentation for review in a timely manner. Of 256 Masonic hall associations
in the last five years, Masonic Properties Committee received 45 applications

Many brothers elected to Masonic hall associations by constituent lodges do

The duty of the Committee on Masonic Properties is to provide such expertise
via legal analysis to ensure contracts for improvements are written appropriately
and cover important details, such as properly defining the involved parties, the
scope of work, insurance requirements, and any appropriate legal remedies in
the event of breach of contract. Failure to seek appropriate counsel from the
committee has resulted in financial harm to lodges and hall associations without
recourse. Additionally, the committee reviews the overall financial standing
of the lodge or hall association to ensure adequate capital is available in the
event of unforeseen additional costs. The committee has experienced many
situations in which a lodge or hall association has over-extended its financial
abilities when entering a contract for a given project.
It is up to this voting body to determine whether the convenience of not
consulting the Committee on Masonic Properties on projects under $50,000
is worth the additional financial and legal risks.

Resolution 22-04
This resolution would increase the threshold amount of a contract requiring
approval from the Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic Properties. Specifically,
this resolution would amend the California Masonic Code section 406.060(D)
to state $50,000 instead of $25,000.
The CMC currently requires the Committee on Masonic Properties to examine and approve all details regarding any contract involving a lodge, Masonic hall
a ssociation, committee, partnership or corporation, or other entity representing
itself to be Masonic in character, or operating for the benefit of a lodge or lodges
in this jurisdiction for a contract for or commencement of the construction,
alteration, improvement, replacement, repair or other maintenance of real
property if the expected cost is in excess of $25,000.
Hall associations are not allowed to re-classify a project into a series of
smaller projects for the purpose of keeping costs under the $25,000 threshold
in the same budgetary year.
The Committee on Masonic Properties requires, at the time of application,
minutes of the lodge or hall association containing the approval for the project, current lodge or hall association bank statements, three competitive bids,
complete design and engineering report approved by relevant authorities, time
required to complete the project, warranty terms, and contractors’ certificate of
insurance as well as other applicable insurance required to complete the project.
Proponents contend that monetary inflation has increased the costs for
services that in the past would have been under the current threshold. The
$25,000 threshold was adopted in the year 2000, which adjusted for inflation,
approximates to $43,000 in today’s dollars.

of submissions to the committee, allowing for more expeditious approval of
